units.tr: by which the mind is bound to the body, since it was not permitted to loosen it.
(The knot was not permitted to be loosened.) ## III.

units.la: Necdùm Viro doëto est desperandum, fatetur enim in thesi decima sexta disputationis de Ubicatione Spirituum, quòd si Deus nobis concessisset Ideam positivè repræsentantem quid substantia sit Spiritualis etiam absq; relatione ad extrinseca, tum facilè conciperemus modum, quo Spiritus sunt in loco; Unde sic colligo, Atqui Deus nobis dedit Ideam, quâ mens seipsam accuratissimè novit; Ergo facilè intelligimus modum quo animus corpori est unitus; Quid enim animus est nisi substantia cogitans?
units.tr: Nor is the learned man yet to be despaired of, for in thesis sixteen of the disputation on the Location of Spirits he admits that if God had granted us an idea positively representing what a spiritual substance is, even apart from its relation to external things, then we would easily conceive the mode in which spirits are in a place. Hence I reason thus: But God has given us an idea by which the mind knows itself most accurately; therefore we easily understand the mode by which the mind is united to the body. For what is the mind but a thinking substance? ## IV.

units.la: In confesso quidem apud nos est. Primò quod corpori mens non est unita partibus suis extremis ad instar corporum duorum; Tùm quia animo nullæ sunt partes quibus corpori adhærescat; Animus enim intelligit, imaginatur, recordatur, vult, sentit, & sic varijs modis cogitat; Id verò quod partes habet est divisibile, in varias figuras torqueri patitur, ut modò sit triangulare, modò quadrangulare, &c. modò rarum, modò densum, &c. quæ attributorum summa differentia docet, quod cum cogitatione partium communio in unam eandemq; rem convenire non possit: Tùm quia animus hunc contactum sentiret; Quicquid enim vel leviter corpus afficit, id quidem sentit animus, quantò magis ergò hunc animus sentiret contactum, quo non posset non vehementius affici? Quid quòd in natura rerum æq; arcta unio ac est animi cum corpore non datur? Quæcunq; enim unita sunt, corpora sunt, quæ suis tantùm extremitatibus conjunguntur; Hinc fit ut eorum unum affici possit quanquàm alterum non afficiatur; Corpus verò cui animus est conjunctus, in nulla parte affici potest quin & animus inde afficiatur; cui consequens est quod animus corpori arctiùs fit unitus quàm corpus corpori conjungi possit; Quid quòd ne fingi quidem potest quomodo contactus mutuus, qui animum inter & corpus, possit esse causa cur affecto corpore animus habeat sensum, quin animus hunc contactum ipse sentiat.
units.tr: This is certainly admitted by us. First, the mind is not united to the body by its extreme parts, as two bodies are. Then, because the mind has no parts by which it could adhere to the body: for the mind understands, imagines, remembers, wills, feels, and thinks in various ways. But what has parts is divisible and suffers itself to be turned into various shapes, so that it is now triangular, now quadrangular, and so on, now rare, now dense, and so on, which the sum of these differing attributes shows: community with the thought of parts cannot agree in one and the same thing. Then, because the mind would feel this contact. For whatever affects the body even slightly, the mind indeed feels; how much more, then, would the mind feel this contact, by which it could not but be more strongly affected? Moreover, in the nature of things no union as close as that of mind with body is found. For things that are united are bodies, which are joined only by their extremities; hence it happens that one of them can be affected while the other is not. But the body to which the mind is conjoined cannot be affected in any part without the mind being affected by it. From this it follows that the mind is united to the body more closely than one body can be joined to another. Moreover, it cannot even be imagined how the mutual contact between mind and body could be the cause why, when the body is affected, the mind has sensation, unless the mind itself feels this contact. ## V.

units.la: Imò ipsa natura nobis concessit ideam, quâ intelligimus animum corpori aliter esse unitum, quàm corpus corpori; Verùm enim verò frequens ejus admodùm est abusio, dùm rebus applicatur intelligendis, quibus non debetur; Ita quicunq; qualitates, quæ præter substantiam finguntur ut res, in substantijs ponunt, volunt ejusmodi qualitates substantijs esse arctè unitas, quanquàm eam conjunctionem per superficiei ad superficiem applicationem fieri negent, gnari quod superficies nullas qualitates habeant; Ubi ex consentientium multitudine animadvertimus, Ideæ, quam natura nobis est largita ut animi cum corpore unionem intelligeremus, præposteram fieri applicationem: Tum, quia qualitates ejusmodi non dantur; Tum, quia modus quo substantijs unitas fingunt, debetur animi cum corpore unioni.
units.tr: Indeed nature itself has granted us an idea by which we understand that the mind is united to the body otherwise than body is united to body. But this idea is very often abused when it is applied to things which it does not concern. Thus whoever feign qualities, which are imagined as things apart from substance, place such qualities in substances as being closely united to them, although they deny that this conjunction takes place by the application of surface to surface, knowing that surfaces have no qualities. From the agreement of many we perceive that the application of the idea, which nature bestowed on us so that we might understand the union of mind with body, is made preposterously: first, because qualities of this kind are not given; second, because the mode by which they feign them to be united to substances is owed to the union of mind with body.
VI.

units.la: Secundò in confesso etiam apud nos est, quòd corpori animus non fit unitus cum ulla spatij in corpore suo occupatione, quia animus omnis spatij est expers, id quod patebit ex spatij descriptione.
units.tr: Secondly, it is also granted among us that the soul is not united to the body by occupying any space in its body, since the soul is free of all space, as will be clear from the description of space.
VII.

units.la: Spatium quidem nihil est aliud quàm ipsa corporum extensio abstractè sumpta; Ex quovis proindè corpore, quatenùs extensionem habet, spatium fit.
units.tr: Space is indeed nothing other than the extension of bodies taken abstractly; therefore from any body, insofar as it has extension, space arises.
VIII.

units.la: Proinde eadem est spatij & corporis extensio, alioqui daretur penetratio dimensionum, spatium enim dicitur penetrari â corpore locato.
units.tr: Accordingly, the extension of space and that of body are the same; otherwise there would be a penetration of dimensions, for space is said to be penetrated by a body placed in it.
IX.

units.la: Inter se vero spatia differunt, figurâ, magnitudine, situ inter corpora externa; quæ tria conjunctim sunt sumenda, ut eorum vel uno mutato aliud fit spatium: Ita si spatij figura triangularis, quæ in vase, transijt in quadrangulare, aliud est spatium, & aqua in vase quadrangulari, quod ante triangulare erat, aliud occupat spatium quàm antè; Idq; verum est quanquàm nec vasis magnitudo neq; inter alia corpora situs fuerit mutatus. Eodem modo si spatij magnitudo in vase vel major vel minor facta fuerit, quanquàm prior spatij in vase & figura & situs inter alia corpora salvus sit, tamen inde aliud factum est spatium. Deniq; si situs mutetur inter alia corpora, quanquàm eadem & magnitudo & figura retineatur, aliud est spatium; e.g. ego huic mensæ assidens disto nunc â pariete qui è regione, quatuor pedibus, â pariete verò, quem â tergo habeo sex pedibus; Si fiat ut â pariete, quem ex adverso habui, magis amotus parieti, qui â tergo imminet, propiùs admoveat, mutatus est spatij mei situs ut aliud nunc occupem spatium quàm antea, quanquàm spatij, quod nunc occupo, eadem sit cum spatio priore & magnitudo & figura.
units.tr: Spaces differ from one another in figure, magnitude, and position among external bodies; these three must be taken together, so that if any one of them is changed, the space becomes another. Thus, if the triangular figure of a space in a vessel passes into a quadrangular one, it is a different space, and the water in a quadrangular vessel, which before was triangular, occupies a different space than before; and this is true even though the size of the vessel and its position among other bodies have not been changed. In the same way, if the magnitude of the space in the vessel has become either larger or smaller, although the earlier space in the vessel keeps its figure and its position among other bodies, nevertheless another space has resulted. Finally, if the position among other bodies is changed, although the same magnitude and figure are retained, it is another space; e.g., I, sitting at this table, am now four feet from the wall opposite me and six feet from the wall behind me. If it happens that I move away from the wall that was opposite me and come nearer to the wall that hangs behind me, the position of my space has changed, so that I now occupy a space different from before, although the space I now occupy is the same as the former space in both magnitude and figure.
X.

units.la: Quia etiam corporis natura consistit in extensione quemadmodum spatij, videmus hinc quod corpus â spatio reipsa non differat; Sanè si â corpore omnia abstrahes, quæ ad corporis conceptum necessariò non spectant, facile comperies, corporis remanere ideam, quæ ipsissimi est spatij.
units.tr: Since the nature of body also consists in extension, just as that of space does, we see from this that body does not really differ from space; indeed, if you abstract from body all those things which do not necessarily pertain to the concept of body, you will easily discover that the idea of body remains, which is precisely that of space itself.
XI.

units.la: Interim si quæ inter spatium & corpus sit differentia, illa respondet differentiæ quæ inter genus & speciem; Novimus autem quòd gradus essentiales metaphysici intrinsecè non distinguantur, spatij enim extensionem spectamus ut communiorem, corporis verò quod in spatio est extensionem spectamus ut specialiorem; e. g. Si tollatur lapis è suo spatio, putamus etiam lapidis extensionem inde esse sublatam, utpote quam ut specialiorem & à lapide inseparabilem spectamus; Quanquàm interim arbitremur extensionem spatij in quo erat lapis, remanere eandem sive nunc à ferro sive à ligno sive ab aere sive ab alio quovis corpore occupetur; Quia spatij extensio spectatur generalius, proindeq; eadem esse censetur sive à lapide sive à ligno sive à ferro sive ab aere sive ab alio quovis corpore occupetur, dummodò retineat eandem magnitudinem, figuram & situm inter alia corpora.
units.tr: Meanwhile, if there is any difference between space and body, it corresponds to the difference between genus and species. We know, moreover, that metaphysical essential degrees are not distinguished intrinsically; for we regard the extension of space as the more general, and the extension of the body that is in space as the more special. For example, if a stone is removed from its space, we think that the extension of the stone is also removed with it, since we regard it as more special and inseparable from the stone. Yet meanwhile we judge that the extension of the space in which the stone was remains the same, whether it is now occupied by iron, by wood, by air, or by any other body; because the extension of space is regarded more generally, and is therefore considered the same whether it is occupied by a stone, wood, iron, air, or any other body, provided it retains the same magnitude, figure, and position among other bodies.
XII.

units.la: Et hæc est subtilissimi Cartesij de spatio doctrina, quæ tàm perspicua & solida ut multùm Autori vel solo hoc nomine debeamus; Notum enim est quàm miserè alij de spatij natura fuerint philosophati, ut causa inde Viris alioqui doctis fuerit confitendi neminem mortalium esse qui sciat quid sit spatium.
units.tr: And this is the teaching of the most subtle Descartes concerning space, a doctrine so clear and solid that we owe the author much, if only for this reason alone. For it is well known how wretchedly others have philosophized about the nature of space, so that learned men have been obliged to confess that no mortal knows what space is.
XIII.

units.la: Nuper unus ex Viris Doctis in scenam prodiit, qui, ne Cartesio quicquam debere videretur, doctrinam hanc arrepta undiquè occasione infestavit; Et ut exploratum fiat quàm indignè tantus Philosophus fuerit habitus, paucis ad singula, quibus Philosophi de spatio doctrinâ vexavit, respondebo, ne veritas, postquàm à tanto Philosopho fuit in lucem protracta novis tenebris involuta à conpectu nostro recedat.
units.tr: Recently one of the learned men came forward on the stage, who, so as not to seem to owe anything to Descartes, seized every opportunity to attack this doctrine. And so that it may be made plain how unworthily so great a philosopher has been treated, I will answer briefly, point by point, the objections with which he has harassed the philosopher's doctrine of space, lest the truth, once brought to light by so great a philosopher, be wrapped again in new darkness and withdrawn from our view.
XIV.

units.la: Primò contra Philosophum Vir Doctus ita argumentatur sub finem theseos decimæ quartæ in disputatione prima de Spatio: Dentur, inquit, duo lapides ejusdem magnitudinis & eruatur alter è muro, & alter substituatur in ejus locum mutatur ibi lapis non spatium: Duo sunt lapides unicum spatium quod proinde differt realiter intrinsecè à lapidum extensione. Respondeo conclusio non loquitur de spatio absolutè sumpto, sed de certo & determinato quod à duobus lapidibus successivè occupatur, sciendum verò quòd spatia non ex singulari extensione corporum, à quibus nunc occupantur, sed ex certa magnitudine, figura, situ inter alia corpora fiant singularia, proinde his immutatis idem spatium quodcunq; corpus vel spatium ingrediatur vel è spatio egrediatur, quia spatij extensio est ipsa corporum extensio, sed abstractè sumpta, quæ proinde non variatur variatis corporibus.
units.tr: First, against the philosopher, the learned man argues thus at the end of the fourteenth thesis in the first disputation on Space: "Let there be two stones of the same magnitude, and let one be taken out of the wall and the other put in its place; there is a change of stone, not of space. There are two stones and one space, which therefore differs really and intrinsically from the extension of the stones." I answer: the conclusion does not speak of space taken absolutely, but of a certain and determinate space which is successively occupied by two stones. It should be known, however, that spaces become individual not from the individual extension of the bodies by which they are now occupied, but from a certain magnitude, figure, and position among other bodies. Therefore, with these unchanged, the same space remains whatever body or space enters it or leaves it, because the extension of space is the very extension of bodies, but taken abstractly, which therefore does not vary as the bodies vary.
XV.

units.la: In thesi vicesima nona Vir Doctus hæc habet verba; Spatium intrinsecè & quasi materialiter nullam dicit entitatem, atqz adeò nihil est; Extrinsecè tamen & formaliter includit suo conceptu extensionem corporum locabilium. Ubi Respondeo primò Virum Doctum non differere de spatio sed de eo quod præposterè spacium vocat, quia disputationem habet de eo quod intrinsecè nullam dicit extensionem; Atqui idea spatij non est idea non extensi sed extensi & quidem extensi tantùm; Provoco ad testimonium omnium & literatorum & illiteratorum. Secundò quicunq; hactenùs de spatio disputarunt, in eo convenerunt omnes quòd spatij idea sit tantùm idea extenfi, sed in eo dissentiunt quid illa spatij extensio sit; In qua disquisitione miris vexantur difficultatibus; Vir Doctus illas difficultates tollere & spatij naturam acutè explicare volens non respondet ad id de quo est quæstio, sed ab aliis dissentire volens aliud quid per spatiu intelligit, quàm de quo sit quæstio, dicendo quòd spatium primariò & intrinsecè dicat id quod non est extensum; Disputat ergò de eo quod primariò non est extensum, omnes autem Philosophi contra, quicunq; de spatio disputârunt, disputare voluerunt tantum de eo quod non est nisi extensum; Idq; propterea quia omnes sunt experti & quivis nostrûm est conscius, quòd idea spatij non repræsentet nisi quod extensum est; Sanè fatendum est Viro Docto aut quòd idea spatij falsò repræsentet spatium aut quòd Philosophi ante eum nesciverint quid repræsentaret, prius dici est absurdum, quia, si idea spatij falsò repræsentaret spatium, definiret esse idea spatij; Posterius non minùs est absurdum, quia sic omnis tolleretur cognitio, nam res non aliter cognoscimus quàm intuendo earum ideas; Nec dicat ad spatium extrinsecè pertinere extensionem, ipsa enim conscientia testatur, quòd menti ideam spatij habenti nihil obversetur præterquàm extensio.
units.tr: In thesis twenty-nine the learned man has these words: Space, intrinsically and as it were materially, denotes no entity, and so is nothing; yet extrinsically and formally it includes in its concept the extension of locatable bodies. Here I reply, first, that the learned man is not disputing about space but about what he absurdly calls space, since he holds a debate about what intrinsically denotes no extension. Yet the idea of space is not the idea of the non-extended but of the extended, and of the extended alone. I appeal to the testimony of all, both the learned and the unlearned. Second, all who have hitherto disputed about space have agreed on this, that the idea of space is only the idea of extension, but they differ over what that extension of space is. In this inquiry they are troubled by remarkable difficulties. The learned man, wishing to remove these difficulties and to explain acutely the nature of space, does not answer the question at issue; instead, wishing to differ from others, he understands by space something other than what is in question, saying that space primarily and intrinsically denotes what is not extended. He therefore disputes about what is primarily not extended, whereas all philosophers, whoever have disputed about space, have wished to dispute only about what is nothing but extended. And this is because all have experienced it and each of us is conscious that the idea of space represents nothing but what is extended. Certainly the learned man must concede either that the idea of space falsely represents space, or that the philosophers before him did not know what it represented. The former is absurd, because if the idea of space falsely represented space, it would cease to be the idea of space. The latter is no less absurd, because in that case all knowledge would be destroyed, for we know things only by intuiting their ideas. Nor let him say that extension belongs to space only extrinsically, for consciousness itself testifies that nothing presents itself to the mind that has the idea of space except extension.
XVI.

units.la: Videamus verò quibus argumentis Vir Doctus probare nitatur, quòd spatium intrinsecè dicat negationem extensionis; Ita enim argumentatur thesi tricesimâ: Deus potest annihilare omnia corpora contenta in cubiculo, ut tamen parietes non mutent locum, quo casu patet nihil remansurum inter parietes; Quod si adhuc aliquid extensum tibi fingas, supponamus Deum annihilaturum adhuc illam ipsam quam tibi fingis quantitatem aut entitatem, manentibus semper intactis parietibus. Dictat enim sana ratio & confirmat omni exceptione major revelatio nullum omnino dari ens quod resistere queat omnipotentia divina & quod supremum illud numen destruere non possit. Illud ergo merum nihil quod ab uno pariete ad alterum esse dicimus, est hoc ipsum, quod spatium intrinsecè spectatum vocamus. Respondeo I. Absurdum est omnem omninò extensionem inter duos cubiculi parietes periisse ubi parietes tamen dicuntur inter se distare; Quænam quæso ratio vel fingi potest distantiæ nisi extensio interjecta? Ex. gratiâ, si distant à se mutuò quindecim pedibus, quæ alia ratio esse potest, cur ita à se distent nisi quia latitudo aliqua quindecim pedum interiacet? Fateor nullum parietibus cubiculi interiici posse corpus quod divina virtus non annihilare possit; Verùm enimverò si hoc contingeret parietes fierent sibi mutuò contigui, quia fundamento distantiæ pereunte non potest nö perire distantia: Et implicat contradictionem parietes à se mutuò distantes manere immotos omni extensione, quæ interiacet, pereunte; Perindè enim est ac si dicerem, Deum omnes montes & clivos facere perire manentibus vallibus. II. Si ingenuè agere cupis mecum, mecum fateri necesse habes, quòd nostèr intellectus non possit etiam liberè vagando assequi distantiam duorum parietum quin inter eos aliquam expansionem reipsa esse intelligat; Ut verba, quæ distantiam duorum parietum absquè extensione interiacente affirmant, nullum in loquente sensum reperiant quem interpretentur.
units.tr: Let us see, however, by what arguments the learned man tries to prove that space intrinsically denotes the negation of extension. For he argues thus in thesis thirty: God can annihilate all the bodies contained in a room, while the walls do not change place; in which case it is plain that nothing will remain between the walls. But if you still imagine something extended, let us suppose God annihilating even that very quantity or entity you imagine, the walls always remaining untouched. For sound reason dictates, and a revelation greater than any exception confirms, that there is absolutely no being which can resist divine omnipotence or which that supreme deity cannot destroy. That pure nothing, therefore, which we say lies from one wall to the other, is precisely what we call space when viewed intrinsically. I reply, first: it is absurd that all extension whatever has perished between the two walls of a room, when the walls are nevertheless said to be distant from one another. What reason, I ask, can even be imagined for distance other than the interposed extension? For example, if they are fifteen feet apart from each other, what other reason can there be why they are so distant, unless some breadth of fifteen feet lies between them? I grant that no body can be interposed between the walls of a room which divine power cannot annihilate. But truly, if this happened, the walls would become mutually contiguous, since distance cannot survive once its foundation has perished. And it implies a contradiction that walls mutually distant should remain unmoved while all the extension lying between them has perished. It is just as if I said that God makes all mountains and slopes perish while the valleys remain. Second, if you wish to deal with me ingenuously, you must necessarily concede with me that our intellect, even by wandering freely, cannot grasp the distance between two walls without understanding that some expanse really exists between them. So the words that affirm the distance between two walls without an interposed extension find in the speaker no sense that they could be interpreted to have.
XVII.

units.la: Porrò in thesi tricesima prima ita argumentatur; Supra cælos datur spatium, quia Deus ibi posset locare corpus, sive illud de novo crearet, sive aliquod ex hoc mundo eò transferret; Atqui spatium illud nullam entitatem, nullam extensionem sibi intrinsecam habet; Postea pergit in eadem thesi prolixius probando, quòd spatium, quod est extra mundum, nullam habeat extensionem. Respondeo primò, nemini licere vel cogitando egredi mundū, quia mundus tantæ est molis, ut quantumvis magnum eum tibi imagineris, major tamen sit tuâ imaginatione; Ut præposterum admodùm sit longiùs velle disserere de ijs quæ extra mundum; Et quæcunq; spatia extra mundum fingas, ea pertinent ad mundum ut fines mundi nondum sis egressus ea imaginatus; Idq; patet ex eo, quia quando cogitando tibi videris mundum egressus, tamen extensionum notio tibi nolenti volenti obversatur, quas extensiones ad mundi familiam spectare negare non potes, qui mecum in tuis Disputationibus hinc inde fateris omnem extensionem esse corporis. Secundò, de Deo sanè satis magnificè non sentiunt qui de limitibus mundi aliquid definire audent, & limitatam valdè intellectus sui potentiam ad plura & majora extendere volunt, quàm suam extendere voluit omnipotentiam Creator maximus, caveant hi ne demissos præ se animos ferentes Optimi Conditoris bonitati detractum eant; Quicunque disserere volunt de eo quod extra mundum ponunt perinde faciunt ac si disserere vellent de numero qui ultra maximum, mundus est indefinitæ magnitudinis quemadmodùm numerus.
units.tr: Furthermore, in thesis thirty-one he argues thus: Beyond the heavens there is space, because God could place a body there, whether he created it anew or transferred some body from this world thither. But that space has no entity and no extension intrinsic to itself. Afterwards, in the same thesis, he goes on at greater length to prove that the space which is outside the world has no extension. I reply, first, that no one is permitted to go beyond the world even in thought, since the world is of such magnitude that, however great you imagine it, it is still greater than your imagination. Hence it is quite absurd to wish to argue at length about things outside the world. And whatever spaces you imagine outside the world, they belong to the world, as you have not yet gone beyond its limits in imagining them. This is plain from the fact that when in thought you seem to have passed beyond the world, nevertheless notions of extension present themselves to you whether you will or no, and these extensions you cannot deny belong to the family of the world, since you yourself admit with me in your Disputations, here and there, that all extension belongs to body. Second, they certainly do not think very reverently of God who dare to define anything about the limits of the world and wish to extend the very limited power of their own intellect to more and greater things than the greatest Creator willed to extend his omnipotence. Let these men beware lest, bearing humbled spirits before them, they detract from the goodness of the Best Creator. Whoever wishes to argue about what he places beyond the world acts just as if he wished to argue about a number beyond the greatest; the world is of indefinite magnitude, as number is.
XVIII.

units.la: Insuper in thesi tricesima secunda ita argumentatur; Spatium in quo collocatus fuit mundus, fuit ante mundum; Atqui spatium illud nullam habuit entitatem; Ergo concludit spatium intrinsecè esse nihil; Postea in eadem thesi prolixè probat, quòd spatium illud nullam habuerit entitatem. Respondeo I. Ante mundum nullum fuit spatium, sed cum corporibus postea demùm fuit concreatum. II. Nullum lum etiam fuit Ubi ante mundum, in quo mundus collocaretur; Ubi enim dicit situm corporis inter alia corpora; Ergo nullo existente corpore nullum est Ubi, in quo corpus collocari possit.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the thirty-second thesis he argues as follows: The space in which the world was placed was before the world; but that space had no entity; therefore he concludes that space is intrinsically nothing. Afterwards, in the same thesis, he proves at length that this space had no entity. I answer: first, there was no space before the world, but it was created together with the bodies only later. Second, there was not even any "where" before the world in which the world could be placed. For where he speaks of the position of a body among other bodies, the where is therefore presupposed; so, with no body existing, there is no where in which a body could be placed.
XIX.

units.la: Praevidit Vir Doctus priorem responsionis partem, unde eam praeoccupat in thesi tricesima tertia, in qua ostendere conatur quod spatium non posset dici concreatum cum corporibus; Hoc argumento; Si spatium suisset concreatum cum corporibus tunc spatium esset aliquid reale diversum a corporibus, quia, inquit, Id quod creatur cum alio est aliquid reale diversum ab eo cum quo creatur. Verum quid contendam pluribus cum mera in ratiocinatione sit logomachia. Spatiu enim dicitur concreatu cum corporibus, non quod alia creationis actione spatia, alia vero corpora fuerint facta, nam eadem creatione, qua corpora fuerunt producta, etiam ipsa fuerunt producta spatia; Spatium enim & corpus plane una & eadem est res; Ergo non requiruntur distinctas creandi actiones: Quemadmodum Ens, Substantia, Corpus dicuntur creata cum Terra, non quod alia creandi actione Ens, alia Substantia, alia Corpus, alia Terra fuerit facta; Sed quia sunt gradus essentiales metaphysici, & proinde una & eadem res, producta sunt simul una & eadem creatione.
units.tr: The learned man foresaw the first part of this reply, and so he anticipates it in the thirty-third thesis, where he tries to show that space could not be said to be created together with bodies, by this argument: If space had been created together with bodies, then space would be something real, distinct from bodies, because, he says, that which is created together with another is something real, distinct from that with which it is created. But why should I contend at length here, when such reasoning is mere logomachy? For space is said to be created together with bodies not because space was made by one act of creating and bodies by another. Rather, by the same creation by which bodies were produced, space itself was also produced; for space and body are plainly one and the same thing. Therefore distinct acts of creating are not required. In the same way, being, substance and body are said to be created together with earth, not because being was made by one act of creating, substance by another, body by another, and earth by another; but because they are metaphysical essential grades, and so, being one and the same thing, they were produced at once by one and the same creation.
XX.

units.la: In thesi tricesima quarta ait, entia non esse multiplicanda praeter necessitatem, nullam vero necessitatem esse statuendi spatium intrinsece esse ens; Patet. 1. Quia commode aliter explicari potest quid sit. 2. Contra requiritur ut nihil sit, ubi enim nihil est, facile locari queunt corpora & contra ubi jam est aliquid extensum, alia locari nequeunt. Respondeo primo, Nihila minus sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem quàm entia, quia ex multitudine Nihilorum periculum oritur ne mundus pereat, ex multitudine verò entium aucta augetur mundus. Secundò entia non magis multiplicamus quàm Vir Doctus, quia extensionem, quam vocamus spatium, esse ens fatetur Vir Doctus: Ad rationem verò priorem respondeo. 1. Quòd definiendo spatium per Nihil non indicetur quid sit, sed quid non sit, scil. non ens. 2. Ex posterioribus patebit quòd per Nihil nullo modo explicari possit quid sit spatium intrinsecè. Ad posteriorem verò rationem dico a. Nihil non posse esse spatium, quia Nihil tollitur præsente corpore, atqui spatium non tollitur corpore, nam corpus est in spatio: Si velis τὸ Nihil servari ubi corpus est; Ergo τὸ Nihil quod fuit ante mundum, adhuc est in mundo, quia in eo tanquàm in spatio, vis positum esse mundum: Sic salsissimum erit id, quod in confesso est apud omnes sanæ mentis homines, quòd inter Ens & Nihil sit infinita distantia non tantùm Metaphysica sed etiam Mathematica. b. In Nihilo non potest locari corpus, quia in Nihilo non est ubi locetur; Ita ut neq; Deus corpora hujus mundi in Nihilo collocaverit, sed in spatio quod condendo corpora condidit; Nec spatium in Nihilo collocatum dici potest, Tùm, quia spatiorum singularium situs primùm designatur ubi quodvis corpus delitescat, situs autem absolvitur solâ vicinià & distantiâ, quam spatia singularia erga se invicem habent: Tùm, quia quodvis corpus locatur in extenso, quodvis enim corpus locandum suam habet extensionem, in qua locari solet, quæ ubicunq; est spatium est; ut corpus locari proindè non possit nisi in extenso, quod ab ipso corpore locato tamen intrinsecè non differt.
units.tr: In the thirty-fourth thesis he says that beings are not to be multiplied beyond necessity, and that there is no necessity for holding that space is intrinsically a being. This is shown: (1) because what it is can be explained otherwise in a convenient way. (2) On the contrary, it is required that there be nothing where there is nothing, for bodies can easily be placed where there is nothing; but where something extended already exists, other things cannot be placed. I answer first: nothings are no less to be multiplied beyond necessity than beings, because from a multitude of nothings danger arises that the world might perish, whereas from a multitude of beings the world is increased. Second, we do not multiply beings any more than the learned man does, since the learned man himself admits that the extension we call space is a being. To the first reason I answer: (1) by defining space through nothing, one does not indicate what it is, but what it is not, namely, not a being. (2) From what follows it will be clear that what space intrinsically is cannot in any way be explained through nothing. To the second reason I say, a. Nothing cannot be space, because nothing is removed when a body is present; but space is not removed by a body, for a body is in space. If you wish the Nothing to be kept where the body is, then the Nothing which was before the world is still in the world, because you want the world to be placed in it as in space. Thus it will be most absurd what is granted by all men of sound mind, that between Being and Nothing there is an infinite distance, not only metaphysical but also mathematical. b. A body cannot be located in nothing, because in nothing there is no place where it could be located. So God did not place the bodies of this world in nothing, but in space, which he made when he created the bodies. Nor can space be said to be placed in nothing. Then, because the position of individual spaces is first designated by where any body lies hidden, and position is determined solely by the nearness and distance which individual spaces have toward one another. Then, because any body is located in what is extended; for every body to be located has its own extension, in which it is customarily located, and wherever that is, there is space. So a body cannot be located except in what is extended, which nevertheless does not differ intrinsically from the located body itself.
XXI. On
XXI.

units.la: Deindè in thesi quinta disputationis secundæ de spatio his inter alia utitur verbis; Quoad Cartesium, multò minùs poterit dicere corpus mutare locum internum, quem statuit esse ipsammet extensionem corporis.
units.tr: Next, in thesis five of the second disputation, on space, he uses among other things these words: "As far as Descartes is concerned, he will be much less able to say that a body changes its internal place, which he holds to be the very extension of the body."

units.la: Respondeo primò, ex his verbis colligo, quòd Cartesium, quantum par est, non fueris meditatus, quia scires quòd Cartesius spatia faciat inter se distincta situ, magnitudine ac figurâ, cui consequens necessariò est, quòd corpora sua spatia mutent sive situm sive magnitudinem sive figuram mutent. Secundò, mihi gravissima causa est cur credam ex tua hypothesi, quâ spatium intrinsecè sumptum putas esse Nihil, nunquam posse ostendi quòd ullum corpus suum spatium intrinsecè sumptum mutare possit, nam quomodò mutaret cùm Nihil à Nihilo non differat? Quomodò ex uno Nihilo in aliud transire corpus dici potest?
units.tr: I reply first that from these words I gather you have not studied Descartes as carefully as you should, since you ought to know that Descartes makes spaces distinct from one another by their situation, magnitude and figure. It follows necessarily that bodies change their space whenever they change their situation, magnitude or figure. Second, I have a very weighty reason for believing that, on your hypothesis, by which you hold that space taken intrinsically is Nothing, it can never be shown that any body can change its own space taken intrinsically. For how would it change, since Nothing does not differ from Nothing? How can a body be said to pass from one Nothing into another?
XXII.

units.la: In thesi nona abundè Cartesianis satisfacere sibi videtur ubi inter alia ait; Fatendum est mentem in loco interno distinguere terminum aliquem in quo sit corpus à corpore ipso. Atqui adeò cùm terminus ille sit non ens, vim quandam menti esse attendendi ad τὸ Nihil. Respondeo, terminum illum non esse Nihil quod locum corporum designet, quia talis essectus est realis, qui à Nihilo non potest proficisci, cùm causa non possit effectu esse toto genere ignobilior, & Nihili nulla sint effecta: Deindè quia quandò mens terminum, in quo sint corpora, attendit, homo cum indice monstrare potest dicendo hic vel ibi; atqui Nihil non potest monstrari digito, quia inter nihil & hominem major est distantia, quàm digito monstrari possit: Insuper quomodò Nihil monstrari digito potest, cùm tibi fatendum sit, quòd
units.tr: In the ninth thesis he seems to satisfy the Cartesians fully, where among other things he says: It must be admitted that the mind, in internal place, distinguishes some boundary in which the body is from the body itself. But since that boundary is a non-being, there is a certain power in the mind of attending to the Nothing [τὸ Nihil]. I answer that this boundary is not Nothing designating the place of bodies, because such an effect is real, and it cannot proceed from Nothing, since a cause cannot be wholly baser in kind than its effect, and Nothing has no effects. Next, because when the mind attends to the boundary in which bodies are, a man can point to it with a finger, saying here or there; but Nothing cannot be pointed out with a finger, because the distance between nothing and a man is greater than any finger can point across. Moreover, how can Nothing be pointed out with a finger, since you must admit that

units.la: ibi, ubi mentis radii terminantur, aliquid fit, tum, quia totus mundus est plenus, tum quia Nihil perit ibi ubi est aliquid: Id vero quod mens attendit tanquam terminum corporis est spatium aliquod in quo corpus est tanquam in suo loco interno; Spatium vero ipsum in nullo est loco cum sit ipse locus; Si vero & spatia dicuntur esse alicubi, denominatio desumpta est a situ, quem spatia inter sese habent sua vicinia & distantia. In eadem thesi pergit Vir Doctus. Nisi intra corpus attendamus Nihil, in quo tanquam in termino sit corpus, nunquam satisfaciemus modis loquendi & concipiendi, qui tamen veri sunt non falsi; Non enim dicimus corpus ipsum esse locum, aut locum ipsum moveri, sed corpus esse in loco & moveri per locum etiam internum. Respondeo, hae locutiones nobis minime obsunt, spatium enim distinguitur a corpore ut genus a specie, ut spatium abstracte magis sumatur quam corpus; Unde hae vulgares locutiones spatium non esse ipsum corpus, sed corpus esse in spatio, & corpus moveri in spatio. Pergit praeterea; Imo evidenter mens nostra attendit ad illum terminum in quo sunt dimensiones corporis, & quem spectat tanquam invariatum, etsi corpora sibi invicem in eo succedant, imo etsi nullum in eo fuerit corpus. Respondeo, terminus tuus nihil est praeter extensionem corporum abstracte sumptam, quae, quia abstracte sumitur, invariata manet, quaecunque corpora in eo sibi succedant; Si vero contingeret ut in termino, quem attendis, nullum foret corpus, tunc nec ipse maneret terminus, in quo corpora sibi mutuo successerant; Nam, quod probe notandum, quanquam locus internus perinde se habet ad quodvis recipiendum corpus, tamen ex eo tantum constituitur, a quo in praesens occupatur, sed quia successive ex quovis constitui potest, fit, ut extra omne corpus locum internum constitui posse putent, id quod cum errore putant. Progreditur, ut si quis de ponte in flāentum prospicit, radij mentis ejus non minus quam oculorum fixe attendunt ad terminum, per quem fluit aqua, quem novit remanere, etsi nulla foret aqua aut aliud corpus. Respondeo, illum terminum, per quem aqua fluit nolens volens cum extensione intelligis, & quia fateris omnem extensionem esse corporis, vides quomodo ille terminus nihil aliud sit quam extensio corporum sed in genere sumpta; Fateor quod ille terminus remaneret omnino, etsi nulla foret aqua, quia sequeretur aer vel aliud aliquod corpus, quod aeque extensionem haberet ac aqua, in cujus extensione conservaretur: Quemadmodum humanitas, quanquam in quocunq; homine una & eadem sit res cum homine, tamen conservari potest vel in uno solo homine, quam reliqui omnes, in quibus erat, perijssent: Ita terminus, in quo tanquam in loco interno collocas corpus, extensionem habet, sed quae est ipsa extensio corporis a quo occupatur; Et haec extensio termini conservari potest in quovis corpore, a quo occupari potest quatenus quodvis corpus suam extensionem habet. Pergit ulterius; Nec situs nec corpus ipsum locatum potest repleri, sed illud Nihil. Respondeo 1. Si Nihil posse putas evacuari & repleri nolens volens Nihilo laxitatem tribuis, quae etiam secundum te est corporis non Nihili: Nec dicas laxitatem tribui Nihilo extrinsecè respectu corporis locabilis, Nam si Nihil putas corpore posse repleri non potes non laxitatem tribuere Nihilo ante corpus locabile, & Nihili laxitas est causa cur corpus in eo tanquam in spatio poni posse putas: Nec vel fingere potes quomodo Nihil corpore replendum non habeat laxitatem ante corpus quo replendum est. 2. Nihil repleri posse est contradictio manifesta, nam plenitudine tollitur Nihil; Absurdiffimum etiam est Nihilum remanere ubi corpus èst,quia Nihil omnia negat; Abfurdiffimum est in Nihilo aves volare & pisces natare, quia illæ suis alis, hi suis pinnis tangerent Nihil, dùm non nisi corpus tangi potest; Pisces etiam natatu & aves volatu describerent lineas in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio, & sic Nihil erit extensum, quia in eo lineæ duci possunt; Duo corpora nunquàm poterunt fe mutuò tàm arctè amplecti quàm Nihil & corpus fe mutuò fovent, quia in spatio corpus est cum penetratione; Et quodcunque Malagma morbo applicetur, hæc absurda sequi ex sententia, quâ Nihilum ponitur spatium in quo corpora existant, quilibet videt; Quivis enim secum perpendat, an non Nihilo laxitas tribuatur, fi statuatur in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio omnia corpora esse posita. Pergit Vir Doctus, ut porrò probet Nihil revera spatium esse: Quamvis Deus nulla creaffet corpora, aut fi hodiè destrueret, v. g. aërem, tamen Angeli possent esse in illo Nihilo. Refpondeo primò, fateor, quòd fi Deus nulla creaffet corpora, tunc vice corporum Nihil effet, sed quia corpora Deus fecit sic vice Nihili corpora sunt, ut proindè in mundo Nihil non fit reperire, quia ejus vice mundus est; Secundò, fi Angeli sunt in Nihilo, ergò nufpiàm sunt, quia Nihil nufpiàmeft; Tertiò, fi Angeli sunt ubi Nihil est, tunc Angeli sunt Nihil; Quartò, quomodò Angeli possunt esse in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio, cùm ipse spatium confideres per relationem ad corporis locabilis capacitatem? Quintò, Angeli funtSpiritus, spatium verò est ipsa corporum extensio; Ergò Angeli egent spatio in quo existant, quomodò corpore. Pergit argumentando contra Cartefium; Cogitur Cartefius gravissima nostro judicio absurda admittere, nempè. 1. Locum v. g. hujus cubiculi, ne divinâ quidem virtute vacuum esse posse. 2. Mundum nullos habere fines fines magnitudinis suæ; Atq; adeò Deum ne quidem unum corpus creare posse supra Cælos, multò minùs creare posse plures mundos; Item nec Deum posse totum mundum vel tantillum movere secundùm lineam rectam, alias videt locum dari sine corpore. Respondeo primò, in his tuis argumentis clarè ostendis quòd Cartesij principia tibi nondum sint cognita, quia Cartesio in more positum non est quicquam de potentia Dei infinita definire, cùm sciat intellectum nostrum esse finitum, Dei verò potentiam infinitam; Considerat duntaxat quid à nobis possit percipi vel nō possit, & cavet diligenter ne judicium ullũ à perceptione dissentiat; Quapropter audacter affirmat, Deum posse id omne, quod possibile esse percipimus; Non autem è contrario audacter negat Deum posse id quod conceptui nostro repugnat, sed dubitat tantùm an Deus id possit. Secundò, ita fatetur absurdum esse & implicare contradictionem locum cubiculi esse vacuum & parietes cubiculi inter se distare, sed an non Deus id facere possit, quod fieri absurdum est rationi Cartesius non definit sed dubitat; Et sanè absurdissimum esse parietes cubiculi inter se distare, quanquam nulla latitudo interiaceat, quivis rationis compos clarè videt; Omnis distantia est relatio, omni relationi est fundamentum aliquod, distantiæ verò, ubi parietes e. g. quindecim pedes inter se distant, quæ alia quæsò ratio vel fingi potest quàm quòd latitudo quindecim pedum parietibus interjecta est? Vir verò Doctus, ut Cartesio Summo Philosopho refragari possit hoc delirium defendit, quòd parietes duo inter se possint distare quanquàm nulla latitudo sit interʃita, satis esse, inquit in thesi vicesima quinta, quòd latitudo aliqua interponi possit; Sed sciat volo quòd cùm distantiæ duorum parietum fundamentum sit latitudo interjecta, distantia, quæ actu est, requirat etiam latitudinem quæ actu sit interposita, non vero quæ tantum interponi possit; Quid quòd ne fingi potest quomodò inter duos parietes revera nunc distantes latitudo poni possit quin revera sit posita? Si fundamentum distantiæ esse putas quòd parietes se non contingunt, est petitio principij, quia hoc est in quæstione, nempe quodnam sit fundamentum quòd se mutuò non contingant, nam hæc sunt synonyma, corpora se non contingunt; Corpora à se mutuò distant. Mirum est quòd nostra ratio distantiæ vel negati contactus à te non adoptatur, quæ rem tam clarè explicat, e. g. Si quæro cur Berna distet Lausannâ, quæ aptior ratio reddi potest, quàm quòd Bernæ atq; Lausannæ latitudo quædam interjacet? Secundùm Viri Docti hypothesin fieri potest, ut Berna distet Lausannâ itinere duorum dierum, quanquàm longitudo nulla actu interjaceat; Quò casu tabellarius suò frustraretur stipendiò, & vinum vestri agri transferri Bernam posset absq; portorio, quæ transvehendi ratio sanè multò esset compendiosior quàm per canales; Eodem casu discipulus in suo themate committeret barbarismum, si distantiam, quam duæ illæ Urbes inter se habent, latinè exprimere volens diceret Berna distat Lausannâ longitudine itineris duorum dierum, quia nec itinera nec longitudo ulla interjaceret. Tertiò, ut ad secundum absurdum, quò premere Cartesium conaris, respondeam; Cartesij sententia non est, mundum nullos habere fines, sed nos vel cogitando fines mundi assequi non posse, an verò reipsa fines habeat nec ne non definit sed dubitat, quia quantumvis magnum mundum nobis imaginemur, majorem adhuc esse reperinus; Ita ut absurdum sit omninò rationi extra mundum poni corpus posse; Quemadmodùm absurdum est rationi extra numerum maximum poni numerum posse: Etiam absurdum est rationi plures mundos esse posse, nam mundi, quos supponis esse posse extra hunc mundum, vel distant ab hoc mundo vel non; Si prius, corpus esse oportet, quô interiacente hic ab illis distet, illud corpus cum ijs, quæ ipsi sunt contigua, spectant ad hunc mundum, ut sic non componant nisi unum mundum; Si posterius; Etiam non componunt nisi unum mundum, nam mundus complectitur ea omnia, quæ ipsi sunt contigua, tum quia mundus est τὸ πᾶν, tum quia aliâs alius mundus esset Terra, alius Aër, alius Aqua, &c. Absurdum etiam est rationi totum mundum moveri posse, quia totum mundum sibi imaginari non potest homo, cùm nullos assequi fines cogitando possit.
units.tr: There, where the rays of the mind terminate, something comes to be, both because the whole world is full, and because nothing perishes where something is. What the mind attends to as the limit of a body, however, is some space in which the body is, as in its own internal place. But space itself is in no place, since it is itself place. If spaces are also said to be somewhere, the designation is taken from the position which spaces have among themselves in their nearness and distance. The learned man continues on the same thesis: Unless we attend within the body to Nothing, in which the body is as in its limit, we shall never satisfy the modes of speaking and conceiving, which are nevertheless true and not false; For we do not say that the body itself is place, or that place itself is moved, but that the body is in place and is moved through internal place as well. I reply that these expressions do us no harm. For space is distinguished from body as genus from species, in that space is taken more abstractly than body. Hence these common expressions: that space is not the body itself, but that the body is in space, and that the body is moved in space. He goes on: Indeed our mind plainly attends to that limit in which the dimensions of the body are, and which it regards as unchanged, even though bodies succeed one another in it, indeed even if no body were in it. I reply that your limit is nothing but the extension of bodies taken abstractly, which, because it is taken abstractly, remains unchanged, whatever bodies succeed one another in it. But if it happened that in the limit you attend to there were no body, then the limit itself would not remain, in which the bodies had succeeded one another. For, as must be carefully noted, although internal place stands in the same relation to any body whatever that is received, yet it is constituted only from that by which it is at present occupied; but because it can be constituted successively from any body, it comes about that people think an internal place can be constituted outside every body, which they think with error. He proceeds: As when someone looks down from a bridge into a river, his rays of mind no less than of eyes are fixed on the limit through which the water flows, which he knows remains even if there were no water or other body. I reply that you understand that limit through which the water flows, willy-nilly, together with extension; and since you admit that all extension belongs to body, you see how that limit is nothing other than the extension of bodies, but taken in general. I grant that this limit would remain entirely even if there were no water, because air or some other body would follow, which would have extension just as water does, and in whose extension it would be preserved. Just as humanity, although in any man it is one and the same thing with the man, can yet be preserved in one man alone after all the others in whom it was have perished; so the limit in which you place the body as in an internal place has extension, but it is the very extension of the body by which it is occupied. And this extension of the limit can be preserved in any body whatever by which it can be occupied, inasmuch as any body has its extension. He goes on further: Neither position nor the located body itself can be filled, but that Nothing can. I reply, first: if you think Nothing can be emptied and filled, willy-nilly you attribute to Nothing a laxity, which by your own account belongs to body, not to nothing. Nor should you say that laxity is attributed to Nothing extrinsically with respect to the body that can be placed in it. For if you think Nothing can be filled by body, you cannot fail to attribute laxity to Nothing before the body that can be placed, and the laxity of Nothing is the reason why you think a body can be put in it as in space. Nor can you even imagine how Nothing, which is to be filled with body, would not have laxity before the body by which it is to be filled. Second: that Nothing can be filled is a plain contradiction, for by fullness Nothing is removed. It is also most absurd that Nothing should remain where the body is, since Nothing denies all things. It is most absurd that birds should fly and fish swim in Nothing, since the former would touch Nothing with their wings and the latter with their fins, whereas only body can be touched. Fish too, in swimming, and birds, in flying, would describe lines in Nothing as in space, and so Nothing would be extended, since lines can be drawn in it. Two bodies could never embrace one another as closely as Nothing and body cherish one another, since in space body is with penetration. And whatever plaster is applied to the disease, anyone can see that these absurdities follow from the opinion by which Nothing is posited as the space in which bodies exist. Let anyone consider whether laxity is not attributed to Nothing, if it is held that all bodies are placed in Nothing as in space. The learned man continues, in order to prove further that Nothing is really space: Even if God had created no bodies, or if he were today to destroy, for example, the air, nevertheless angels could be in that Nothing. I reply, first, I grant that if God had created no bodies, then Nothing would be in place of bodies; but since God made bodies, bodies are thus in place of Nothing, so that in the world no Nothing is to be found, because the world is in its place; second, if angels are in Nothing, then they are nowhere, because Nothing is nowhere; third, if angels are where Nothing is, then angels are Nothing; fourth, how can angels be in Nothing as in space, when you consider space itself through its relation to the capacity of a locatable body? Fifth, angels are spirits, but space is the very extension of bodies; therefore angels need a space in which to exist, just as bodies do. He goes on arguing against Descartes: Descartes is compelled to admit things most absurd in our judgment, namely: 1. that the place, for example, of this room cannot be empty even by divine power. 2. that the world has no limits of its magnitude; and therefore that God cannot create even one body beyond the heavens, much less create several worlds; likewise that God cannot move the whole world, or even a little, in a straight line, otherwise there would be place given without body. I reply, first, in these arguments of yours you plainly show that the principles of Descartes are not yet known to you. For it is not Descartes's custom to define anything about the infinite power of God, since he knows that our understanding is finite and God's power infinite. He considers only what can or cannot be perceived by us, and takes care that no judgment dissents from perception. Wherefore he boldly affirms that God can do all that we perceive to be possible; but on the contrary he does not boldly deny that God can do what repugnes our concept, but only doubts whether God can do it. Second, he admits that it is absurd and implies a contradiction for the place of a room to be empty while the walls of the room are apart from one another; but whether God cannot do what is absurd to reason, Descartes does not define but doubts. And that it is most absurd for the walls of a room to be apart from one another, though no width lies between them, anyone endowed with reason plainly sees. Every distance is a relation; every relation has some foundation; and in the case of distance, where the walls, for example, are fifteen feet apart, what other reason, I ask, can be imagined than that a width of fifteen feet is interposed between the walls? The learned man, in order to be able to oppose the supreme philosopher Descartes, defends this nonsense, that two walls can be apart from one another though no width is between them: it is enough, he says in thesis twenty-five, that some width can be interposed. But let him know that since the foundation of the distance of two walls is the interposed width, the distance which is actual requires also an actually interposed width, not one that merely can be interposed. What is more, can it not even be imagined how a width could be posed between two walls which are now really distant, without its being really posed? If you think the foundation of distance is that the walls do not touch one another, this is begging the question, because that is what is in dispute, namely what the foundation is that they do not touch one another; for these are synonyms, that bodies do not touch and that bodies are apart from one another. It is remarkable that our account of distance, or of the denial of contact, is not adopted by you; it explains the matter so clearly. For example, if I ask why Bern is distant from Lausanne, what more apt reason can be given than that a certain width lies between Bern and Lausanne? According to the learned man's hypothesis it could happen that Bern is distant from Lausanne by a journey of two days, though no length actually lies between them. In that case the courier would be cheated of his wages, and the wine of your fields could be carried to Bern without toll, a mode of transport certainly much more expeditious than by canals. In the same case a pupil would commit a barbarism in his theme if, wishing to express in Latin the distance which those two cities have between them, he said that Bern is distant from Lausanne by the length of a two days' journey, since neither a journey nor any length would lie between them. Third, let me answer the second absurdity, with which you try to press Descartes. It is not Descartes's opinion that the world has no limits; rather, he doubts whether we can attain the limits of the world either by thinking, or whether it really has limits or not, because however great a world we imagine, we find one still greater. So it is absolutely absurd for reason that a body could be posited outside the world; just as it is absurd for reason that a largest number could be posited outside number. It is also absurd for reason that there could be several worlds, for the worlds which you suppose could be outside this world either are distant from this world or are not. If the former, a body must be between them by which this one is distant from those; that body, together with what is contiguous to it, belongs to this world, so that they make up only one world. If the latter, they also make up only one world, for the world embraces all those things which are contiguous to it, both because the world is [τὸ πᾶν], the whole, and because otherwise there would be one world that was Earth, another Air, another Water, and so on. It is also absurd for reason that the whole world could be moved, since man cannot imagine the whole world to himself, as he cannot attain its limits by thinking.
XXIII.

units.la: Contra Cartesium porrò hæc habet verba in thesi decima sexta; Cartesius errat, quòd credat spatium nihil aliud esse quàm extensionem corporum; Respondeo I. Si Cartesius errat quòd statuit spatium nihil planè esse præter extensionem corporum tunc & tibi merito impingitur idem error, quia & tua est sententia, quòd spatium nihil sit præter extensionem corporum, id quod ita exponitur; Primò doces quòd spatium intrinsecè sit Nihil; Deinde doces quòd spatium extrinsecè dicat ipsam corporum in spatio locabilium extensionem; Ex quibus confici necesse est, ipsum spatium præter extensionem corporum locabilium esse nihil; ut in tuo à Cartesio recedendi conatu videaris haud absimilis homini, qui in curriculo currens magna dierum itinera facere sibi videtur; Nec succenseas mihi quòd tuum spatium nihili facio, sic enim tecum consentio, cùm ipse spatium nihili facias, statuendo illud Nihil esse; Si magnum spatium facerem tibi adversarius viderer, quia spatio nullam vis tribuendam magnitudinem. II. Si attenderes quòd Nihil sit negatio omnis entis corpora non compingeres in Nihil tanquam in pristina. III. Miror quòd perfiftis in renutu cõsentiendi cum Cartefio, cùm te subindè habeat confitentem reum; Annon enim illa tua verba, quæ extant thesi tricesima sexta disputationis secundæ de loco; Tota natura spatij formaliter concepti, quâ spatij, posita est in extensione, nec aliter definiri nec concipi potest; Continent confessionem â reo profeƈtam, quòd sola extensio sit spatium?
units.tr: Further against Descartes you have these words in thesis sixteen: Descartes errs in believing that space is nothing other than the extension of bodies. I reply. I. If Descartes errs in holding that space is nothing at all but the extension of bodies, then the same error is rightly charged against you, since your view too is that space is nothing but the extension of bodies. This you set out as follows: First you teach that space is intrinsically Nothing; then you teach that space extrinsically denotes the extension of bodies locatable in space. From these it must necessarily follow that space itself, apart from the extension of locatable bodies, is nothing. So in your attempt to depart from Descartes you seem not unlike a man running on a race-course who thinks he is making great day-long journeys. Nor be annoyed with me that I make your space nothing; for in this I agree with you, since you yourself make space nothing by declaring it to be Nothing. If I made space something great, I would seem to you an adversary, because no force or magnitude should be ascribed to space. II. If you attended to the fact that Nothing is the negation of every being, you would not place bodies in Nothing as though in their former home. III. I wonder that you persist in refusing to agree with Descartes, when he so often has you confessing as the accused. For do not those words of yours, which stand in thesis thirty-six of the second disputation on place, The whole nature of space, as formally conceived, insofar as it is space, lies in extension, and cannot be defined or conceived otherwise, contain a confession made by the accused that extension alone is space?
XXIV.

units.la: In disputatione tertia de spatio & in disputatione de Ubicatione spirituum tuam sententiam de Nihilo spatij novo temperamento mitigare volens tibi dissimilimus factus es, dùm hinc indeasseris te Nihilum spatij per aƈtum mentis negativum intelligere, intelligendo nihil esse quòd impediat quô minus corpus poni possit; Adeoquè inquis, quandò substantia dicitur esse in spatio, sensus est nihil esse, quo minùs substantia ibi esse possit. Respondeo. Primò, qui phrases tuas examinat, quibus fuisti usus in prima & secunda Disputatione de Loco, non potest non dicere te Nihilum spatij per aƈtum mentis positivum intellexisse; Annon enim hæ fuerunt tuæ phrases? Omnia corpora existunt in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio. Omnis motus fit in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio. Aves volant & pisces natant in Nihilo tanquàm spatio. Fluenta fluunt per Nihilum tanquàm per spatium. Mundus ipse est collocatus in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio. Ex quibus tuis phrasibus quis non colligit te Nihilum spatij per aƈtum mentis positivum intellexisse? Secundò; Non dubito quin tua diuturnior rei meditatio aliorumq; contra te argumentandi diligentia, Spatium aliud quid esse te docuerint, quàm in prima & secunda disputatione videaris credidisse; Pudore tamen erroris dučtus sententiam immutare quàm revocare maluisti. Tertiò; Efficacior est spatij significatio quàm ut tantùm neget impedimentum corporis locandi, significat enim præterea capacitatem corporis locandi. Quarto; Ipsa extensio abstractè sumpta negat impedimentum locandi corporis. Quinto, Imò extenfio abstractè sumpta præterea habet recipiendi corpus capacitatem; Ergo sola illa extensio abstractè sumpta est spatium; Quòd verò extensio abstractè sumpta capacitatem habeat recipiendi corpus patet ex eo,quia in corpore recepto confervatur, quomodò humanitas in Petro vel Paulo,&c. conservari solet. Sexto; Hac ratione, quæso attende, non explicas quid fit spatium intrinsecè sumptum, sed tantùm quid non fit, genuina enim mentis tuæ interpretatio est,quòd spatium intrinsecè non fit aliquid quod impediat locationem corporis; At verò hæc explicatio neq; indicat spatium esse nihil,neq; esse aliquid, sed simpliciter de spatio negat quòd impediat locationem corporis; Ita ut clarissimè nunc videas, quòd tibi diffimilimus in posterioribus disputationibus fis factus, nam in prioribus nihil inculcasti Lectori crebriùs quàm spatium intrinsecè esse Nihil; Nunc verò ea ratione tuam mentem mitigas, quâ spatium nihil an aliquid fit tacetur. Septimò; Miror jam quid tuum fit spatium, cùm ex tua mutata sententia factum fuerit ut neq; fit aliquid neq; nihil; Ejusmodi strigosum monstrum Affrica tulit nunquàm; Ita prolixissimis tuis disputationibus tandem effecisti ut spatium album an atrum fit nesciatur.
units.tr: In your third disputation on space and in the disputation on the location of spirits, wishing to soften your view that space is Nothing by a new qualification, you have become quite unlike yourself. You have since asserted that you understand the Nothing of space through a negative act of the mind, understanding it to be the absence of anything that would prevent a body from being placed. And so, you say, when a substance is said to be in space, the sense is that there is nothing that would prevent the substance from being there. I reply. First, anyone who examines the phrases you used in your first and second disputations on place cannot but say that you understood the Nothing of space through a positive act of the mind. Were these not your phrases? All bodies exist in Nothing as in space. All motion takes place in Nothing as in space. Birds fly and fish swim in Nothing as in space. Rivers flow through Nothing as through space. The world itself is situated in Nothing as in space. From these phrases of yours, who does not gather that you understood the Nothing of space through a positive act of the mind? Second, I do not doubt that your longer reflection on the matter, and the diligence of others arguing against you, have taught you that space is something other than what you seemed to believe in the first and second disputations. Yet, led by shame at your error, you preferred to change your opinion rather than retract it. Third, the meaning of space is more forceful than merely denying an impediment to placing a body; for it further signifies the capacity to receive a body. Fourth, extension taken in the abstract itself denies an impediment to placing a body. Fifth, indeed, extension taken in the abstract further has the capacity to receive a body. Therefore that extension taken in the abstract alone is space. That extension taken in the abstract has the capacity to receive a body is evident from the fact that it is preserved in the body received, as humanity is usually preserved in Peter or Paul, and so on. Sixth, by this reasoning, please attend, you do not explain what space is when taken intrinsically, but only what it is not. For the genuine interpretation of your mind is that space intrinsically is not something that impedes the location of a body. But this explanation neither indicates that space is nothing, nor that it is something; it simply denies of space that it impedes the location of a body. So you can now see very clearly that you have become quite unlike yourself in your later disputations. For in the earlier ones you impressed upon the reader, more often than anything else, that space intrinsically is Nothing; but now you soften your view by a form of words under which it is left unsaid whether space is something or nothing. Seventh, I now wonder what your space is, since by your changed opinion it has come about that it is neither something nor nothing. Africa has never produced such a lean monster. So, by your very lengthy disputations, you have at last brought it about that it is unknown whether space is white or black.
XXV.

units.la: Fons erroris quo Vir Doctus corpora esse in Nihilo tanquàm in spatio &spatium intrinsecè esse Nihil, est, quòd ideam extensionis abstractè sumptæ, bis applicat ubi non nisi semel applicanda est; Semel enim extensioni corporum abstractè sumptæ & semel spatio, in quo corpora pora sunt locata applicat; Et quia novit extra corporum extensionem nihil esse, inde fit ut spatium intrinsecè putet esse Nihil; Verùm sciat quòd idea extensionis abstractè sumptæ non sit nisi semel applicanda & quidem corporibus locatis; Et fateor nihil proclivius esse quàm ideam extensionis abstractè sumptæ bis applicare, memini enim in hac erronea applicandi consuetudine me diu hæsisse ut crediderim ex. gr. quodvis corpus occupare spatium, quod extra corporis occupantis extensionem suam sibi propriam haberet extensionem, quæ corporis occupantis extensioni esset commensurata; Ex qua vitiosa consuetudine me expedivi quamprimùm subtilissimi Cartesij principiis imbutus discere incepi quid esset corpus, tum enim videns corporis naturam consistere in sola extensione, observavi extra corporis extensionem nullam fingendam esse, quæ spatio sit propria, quia aliâs corporum in spatio fieret penetratio; Quæ consideratio à te sincerà mente volutata tua præjudicia circa spatij Nihilum illicò perire facient.
units.tr: The source of the error by which the learned man holds that bodies are in Nothing, as in space, and that space is intrinsically Nothing, is that he applies the idea of extension taken abstractly twice, where it is to be applied only once. For he applies it once to the extension of bodies taken abstractly, and once to the space in which the bodies are located. And because he knows that outside the extension of bodies there is nothing, he thinks it follows that space is intrinsically Nothing. But let him know that the idea of extension taken abstractly is to be applied only once, and indeed to located bodies. I admit that nothing is more natural than to apply the idea of extension taken abstractly twice. For I remember that I was long stuck in this mistaken habit of application, so that I believed, for example, that any body occupying a space had, outside the extension of the occupying body, an extension of its own, one commensurate with the extension of the occupying body. I freed myself from this faulty habit as soon as, imbued with the principles of the most acute Descartes, I began to learn what body is. For then, seeing that the nature of body consists in extension alone, I observed that no extension is to be imagined outside the extension of the body which would be proper to space, since otherwise there would be penetration of bodies in space. When you consider this with a sincere mind, your prejudices about the Nothingness of space will soon perish.
XXVI.

units.la: Hæc sufficere puto ad vindicandam Nobilissimi Cartesij sententiam, quam de spatio habet; Longa mea respondendi cunctatio argumento esto, quòd in aliorum erroribus confutandis mihi nulla sit delectatio; Interim si veritati à Nobilissimo Cartesio detectæ errores insidiantur, eos amoliri convenit, ne nostra cathedra, in qua Author publicè docetur, infamiam patiatur.
units.tr: I think this is enough to vindicate the opinion of the most noble Descartes concerning space. That my reply has been so long delayed may serve as proof that I take no pleasure in refuting the errors of others. Meanwhile, if errors lie in wait for the truth brought to light by the most noble Descartes, it is fitting to remove them, lest our chair, in which the author teaches publicly, suffer disgrace.
XXVII.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus facilè est videre quòd spatium sit sola corporum extensio abstractè sumpta; proindè ut redeamus unde egressi sumus, animus non potest esse suo corpori unitus cum ulla spatij in corpore occupatione, Cùm enim spatium ab extensione corporis, à quo occupatur, intrinsecè non differat, menti verò nulla sit extensio, spatium sanè nullum occupare mens poterit.
units.tr: From all these things it is easy to see that space is merely the extension of bodies taken abstractly. Therefore, to return to where we started, the soul cannot be united to its body with any occupation of space in the body. For since space does not differ intrinsically from the extension of the body which occupies it, and the mind has no extension, the mind will certainly be unable to occupy any space.
XXVIII.

units.la: Tertio in confesso etiam apud nos est, quòd mens sive animus in suo corpore non sit definitivè, hoc est, totus in toto corpore & totus in qualibet parte corporis, quia hoc intelligi non potest quin mens vel animus in pluralitatem suimet ipsius abijsse cogitetur, id quod absurdum est admodum.
units.tr: Third, it is also admitted among us that the mind or soul is not in its body definitively, that is, whole in the whole body and whole in each part of the body. For this cannot be understood without thinking that the mind or soul has split into a plurality of itself, which is utterly absurd.
XXIX.

units.la: Quarto in confesso etiam apud nos est, quòd mens sive animus in nulla corporis sui parte situm habeat, cùm enim situm faciant sola corpora, etiam solis corporibus debetur, proindè distantiam vel viciniam, quæ inter animum & has vel illas corporis partes, dimetiri, vel etiam spatij, in quo animi sedes sit, magnitudinem vel parvitatem examinare, est absurdissimum.
units.tr: Fourth, it is also admitted among us that the mind or soul has no location in any part of its body. For since only bodies make a location, it belongs to bodies alone; therefore to measure the distance or nearness between the soul and these or those parts of the body, or to examine the size or smallness of the space in which the soul's seat is, is most absurd.
XXX.

units.la: Quinto in confesso etiam apud nos est, quòd mens sive animus in suo corpore non sit, vitam motumq; illi suppeditando; Corpus enim vitæ motuumq; suorum corporalia habet principia, quæ sunt calor in corde delitescens, sanguis per arterias & venas diffusus, spiritusque in nervis toto corpore dispersis, quomodò enim mens vel animus causa esse potest concoctionis vel augmentationis, &c. Cùm plerunq; in nobis contingant mente nescia? Quoties imus, edimus, loquimur mente vel nescia vel reluctante, corpus causa est; Ut audacter affirmem quòd corpus nostrum solum, modò omnia quæ ejus sunt sint illibata, omnes functiones etiam mente separatâ subire possit quas subire solet mente præsente, quanquàm non subiret tàm appositè occasionibus; Ut quod nauta in navi idem sit mens in corpore; Navis motum suum non habet à Nauta, quanquàm motum Nauta dirigat; Ita motum corpus nostrum à mente non accipit, quanquàm eam sui motùs habeat directricem.
units.tr: Fifth, it is also admitted among us that the mind or soul is not in its body supplying it with life and motion. For the body has the corporeal principles of its life and motions: heat lying hidden in the heart, blood diffused through the arteries and veins, and spirits dispersed through the nerves throughout the whole body. For how can the mind or soul be the cause of digestion or growth, etc., when for the most part in us these things happen without the mind's knowledge? When we walk, eat, or speak, the body is the cause, with the mind either ignorant or unwilling. So I boldly affirm that our body alone, provided all its parts remain unimpaired, can perform even with the mind separated all the functions it usually performs with the mind present, although it would not perform them so aptly in response to occasions. Thus the mind is in the body as the sailor is in the ship. The ship does not get its motion from the sailor, though the sailor directs its motion. So too the body does not receive its motion from the mind, though it has the mind as the director of its motion.
XXXI.

units.la: Tandem mens sive animus unitus est corpori suo reciprocatione certarum actionum & passionum, quibus ad se mutuò referuntur; Dùm aliquid fit ab animo quod terminatur ad corpus; Aliquid item fit à corpore quod terminatur ad animum, exempli gratia, mens sive animus vult ut pedes corporis nostri moveantur, indè fit ut revera moveantur; Voluntas mentis est mentis actio, & ipse pedum motus, quatenùs à voluntate imperatus, est corporis passio, quâ actione & passione mens ad corpus & corpus ad mentem ita referuntur ut dicantur unita; Ita ex cogitatione de rebus tristibus fit in corpore quædam molesta variatio; Ubi cogitatio est mentis actio, variatio verò in corpore orta ex illa cogitatione, est corporis passio, quâ actione & passione mens ad corpus & corpus ad mentem ita referuntur ut dicantur unita. Ita vice versâ motus exempli gratiâ oculorum à lumine, aurium ab aëre, manuum ab igne, pedis à lapide in animo confusam perceptionem excitat; ubi motus organorum corporis sunt corporis actiones, perceptiones verò in animo inde ortæ sunt passiones, quibus actionibus & passionibus corpus ad mentem & mens ad corpus ita referuntur ut dicantur unita; Ita mala corporis constitutio sæpè mentem ita assicit ut molesta in animo indè fit perceptio; Ubi depravatio corporis est corporis actio, perceptio verò molesta, quæ indè oritur, est passio, quâ actione & passione corpus ad animum & animus ad corpus ita referuntur ut dicantur indè unita.
units.tr: Finally, the mind or soul is united to its body by a reciprocation of certain actions and passions, by which they refer to each other. While something is done by the soul that terminates in the body, something also is done by the body that terminates in the soul. For example, the mind or soul wills that the feet of our body be moved, and hence they really are moved. The will of the mind is an action of the mind, and the motion of the feet, insofar as it is commanded by the will, is a passion of the body. By this action and passion the mind is referred to the body and the body to the mind in such a way that they are said to be united. Likewise, from thinking about sad things a certain troubling change arises in the body. Here the thinking is an action of the mind, and the change arising in the body from that thinking is a passion of the body. By this action and passion the mind is referred to the body and the body to the mind in such a way that they are said to be united. Conversely, the motions of the organs of the body, for example of the eyes from light, of the ears from air, of the hands from fire, and of the foot from a stone, excite a confused perception in the soul. Here the motions of the bodily organs are actions of the body, and the perceptions arising from them in the soul are passions. By these actions and passions the body is referred to the mind and the mind to the body in such a way that they are said to be united. Thus a bad constitution of the body often affects the mind so that a troubling perception arises in the soul. Here the disorder of the body is an action of the body, and the troubling perception arising from it is a passion, by which action and passion the body is referred to the soul and the soul to the body in such a way that they are said to be thereby united.
XXXII.

units.la: Animus sanè non potest corpori aliter esse unitus quàm eâ ratione quâ à corpore afficitur, quia qnicquid alteri est unitum ab eo ipso unione afficitur; At verò à corpore mens sive animus non potest aliter affici quàm sensationes alias atq; alias indè recipiendo, sive enim corpus secetur, sive trudatur, sive frangatur, sive conteratur, sive cremetur, animus inde nec secatur, nec truditur, nec frangitur, nec conteritur, nec crematur, & tamen indè quoq; afficitur, quomodo? Alias & alias sensationes indè accipiendo; Aliam enim habet animus sensationem quandò corpus secatur, aliam quandò corpus truditur, aliam quandò corpus frangitur, & ita de aliis; Nec ipse animus corpus aliter afficere potest quàm excitando varios in eo motus, quia animus rebus non nisi operativè potest esse præsens. Deindè ipse animus est conscius quòd à vulnere sui corporis acuto dolore revera tangatur; Ut sensus, quò animus ea sentit quæ fiunt in corpore, sit contactus qui animum corpori unit. Insuper animus suâ naturâ est actus ut cessare cogitare non possit quin ipse pereat; Ergò corpori non potest uniri nisi per suos actus.
