Quid quòd quæcunque proprietates vel operationes ex mentis cum corpore conjunctione proficiscuntur, demonstrantur proximè ex substantiæ cogitantis & corporis organici mobilis natura? Si verò vel animus aliter quàm quà cogitans corpori, vel corpus animo aliter quàm quà mobile uniretur, illum arcanum conjunctionis modum proprietates redolerent, quia natura est radix & proprietatum & operationum, quæ rei conveniunt. Tandem eo modo animus est unitus corpori quo à suo corpore tangitur, quandò illud ab alio corpore tangitur, atqui animus à corpore suo non aliter tangitur quandò illud ab alio corpore tangitur, quàm sentiendo corporis sui tactum, quò ab alio tangitur corpore; Ergò animus corpori suo non aliter est unitus, quàm sensu, quò tactum, quò corpus ab alio corpore tangitur, sentit.
units.tr: Certainly the soul cannot be united to the body in any way other than by the mode in which it is affected by the body. For whatever is united to another is affected by that union itself. But the mind or soul cannot be affected by the body except by receiving different sensations from it, one after another. For whether the body is cut, pushed, broken, crushed or burned, the soul is neither cut, pushed, broken, crushed nor burned, and yet it is affected by these things too. How so? By receiving different sensations from them. For the soul has one sensation when the body is cut, another when it is pushed, another when it is broken, and so on with the rest. Nor can the soul itself affect the body except by stirring up various motions in it, since the soul is present to things only operatively. Moreover, the soul is aware that it is truly touched by the sharp pain of a wound in its own body. Thus sense, by which the soul perceives what happens in the body, is the contact that unites the soul to the body. Besides, the soul by its nature is an act, so that it cannot cease to think without perishing. Therefore it cannot be united to the body except through its own acts. Moreover, whatever properties or operations arise from the conjunction of mind with body are shown most immediately from the nature of a thinking substance and of an organic body capable of motion. If, however, the soul were united to the body in some way other than as a thinking thing, or the body to the soul in some way other than as a mobile thing, those properties would betray some hidden mode of conjunction, since nature is the root both of the properties and of the operations that belong to a thing. Finally, the soul is united to its body in the same way in which it is touched by its body, when that body is touched by another body. But the soul is not touched by its own body, when that body is touched by another body, in any other way than by sensing the touch of its own body by which it is touched by another body. Therefore the soul is not united to its own body in any other way than by the sense by which it perceives the body being touched by another body.
XXXIII.

units.la: Objicis Primo, ut animus à corpore affici possit eò modò quò dictum est, necesse est animum corpori priùs unitum esse ut ita indè affici possit; Quemadmodùm corpus à corpore affici nō potest, nisi priùs ei secundùm suam essentiam sit unitum, ut contactus essentiæ præcedat contactum virtutis. Respondeo, procedit hoc argumentum ex eo præjudicio, quo putant res inter se revera uniri non posse nisi quomodò corpus unitur corpori; Quod præjudicium nobis inolevit à teneris, quia toto vitæ nostræ curriculo non observavimus alia unionis genera quàm quæ erant corporum; Si verò perpendatur accuratiùs, quòd animus toto genere distet à corporum conditione, facile est in eam cogitationem incidere, quâ statuitur quòd unio, quæ animum ligat corpori, toto genere à corporum colligatione distet, quia res non possunt non pro naturæ suæ conditione esse conjunctæ.
units.tr: You object, first, that for the mind to be affected by the body in the way just described, it is necessary that the mind be united to the body beforehand, so that it can thence be affected; just as a body cannot be affected by a body unless it is united to it beforehand in its essence, so that contact of essence precedes contact of power. I answer: this argument proceeds from the prejudice by which people think that things cannot truly be united with one another except as body is united with body. This prejudice has grown up in us from childhood, because throughout the whole course of our life we have not observed any kinds of union other than those belonging to bodies. But if we weigh the matter more carefully, namely that the mind differs in its whole kind from the condition of bodies, it is easy to fall into the thought that the union which binds the mind to the body differs in its whole kind from the bodily kind of connection, since things cannot fail to be joined according to the condition of their nature.
XXXIV.

units.la: Objicis Secundo; τὸ operari supponit τὸ esse; Ergò animus in corpore suo operari non posset, nisi ibi priùs esset secundùm suam essentiam. Respondeo 1. Animus suâ naturâ expers est omnis loci; Hic tantùm vel ibi operari potest quò casu ipse hic vel ibi esse dicitur, ut priùs alicubi operetur quàm ibi existat; Interim ubicunq; operativè est revera etiam ipse ibi est; Quòd τὸ operari supponat τὸ esse verum est sensu, quò nihil posse operari quin priùs sit indicatur, falsum verò sensu est quò putatur nihil uspiam operari posset quin ibi priùs res extiterit; Ita
units.tr: You object secondly: "To operate presupposes to be [τὸ operari supponit τὸ esse]. Therefore the soul could not operate in its body unless it were first there according to its essence." I answer, first, that the soul by its nature is free of all place. It can operate here or there only in the sense that it is said to be here or there; so it operates somewhere before it exists there. Meanwhile, wherever it operates, it is really present there too. That operating presupposes being is true in the sense that nothing can operate unless it first exists. It is false in the sense that nothing can operate anywhere unless the thing has first existed there.

units.la: verum est quòd animus operari non possit quin prius sit, falsum verò est quòd nec uspiam operari possit quin prius ibi fuerit. Quòd verò animus suâ natura expers sit omnis loci, patet tum ex eo quia omnis locus efficitur à solis corporibus; Quomodò ergò animus, qui toto genere à corporibus differt, suâ natura ullam haberet relationem ad locum? Tum ex eo, quòd animus suimet ipsius contemplatione vivere ac subsistere potest, quo casu nullus locus, ubi animus subsistat, monstrari potest; Nisi velis, quod absurdum, ipsum animum eo casu esse locum; Tum ex eo quòd animus Metaphysicis dubitationibus, quibus vera Philosophia inchoatur, tentatus dubitat an detur locus, quanquam interim non dubitet quin ipse existat, quô dubitandi casu ostenditur quòd animus suâ natura locum exigat nullum; Tum ex eo, quòd corpora à nostro corpore maximè distantia (nam ab animo nihil distat) animo possunt fieri veré præsentia, quanquàm neque animus ulla peragraverit loca ut corporibus fieret vicinus, neque ipsa corpora nostro corpori propiùs fuerint admota ut animo forent vicina. Tum denique ex eo quòd quicunque locum animo assignant aut fatentur se nescire quomodò sit in loco, aut talia proponunt quæ ab omni sana ratione sunt aliena.
units.tr: It is true that the soul cannot operate unless it first is, but it is false that it cannot operate anywhere unless it has first been there. That the soul by its nature is free of all place is shown, first, because every place is made only by bodies. How then could the soul, which differs from bodies in its whole kind, have any relation to place by its nature? Second, because the soul can live and subsist by contemplating itself, and in that case no place can be pointed out where the soul subsists; unless you wish to say (which is absurd) that the soul itself in that case is a place. Third, because the soul, when it is troubled by the metaphysical doubts with which true philosophy begins, doubts whether any place exists, although meanwhile it does not doubt that it itself exists; in this case of doubting it is shown that the soul by its nature requires no place. Fourth, because bodies most distant from our body (for they are not distant at all from the soul) can become truly present to the soul, although the soul has not traversed any places to become near to the bodies, nor have the bodies themselves been brought closer to our body so as to be near the soul. Finally, because all who assign a place to the soul either confess that they do not know how it is in a place, or propose things that are alien to all sound reason.
XXXV.

units.la: Obijcis Tertio; cùm animus toto genere differat à suo corpore etiam ejus functiones differunt toto genere à functionibus sui corporis, quomodo ergò animi functiones cum functionibus corporis nexum habere possunt, per quem corpori dicatur unitus? Respondeo; Fateor animi & corporis functiones toto genere inter se distare; Unde natura eas copulare nequit, sed sola divinæ voluntatis vis eas in unum conjugium redigit. Ad quam voluntatem Dei tanquam ad sacram anchoram subinde confugere Philosophus ne erubescat; Qui fit enim ut globus meus, postquam tuum loco pepulit, non æquè celeriter pergat moveri quàm antè, quanquàm de suo motu tuo nihil dederit, cùm accidens non migret de subjecto in subjectum? Sanè in solvenda quæstione confugiendum est ad voluntatem Dei, dicendo Deum legem naturæ constituisse, ut corpus, quod alterum loco propellit, de suo motu tantum remittat quantum motûs alterum accepit; Si hujus legis causam aliam quàm Dei voluntatem anquiras in cassum laborabis, quia legum naturæ, cùm sint principia, non alia est explicatio. Et cùm Deus aliarum suarum perfectionum vestigia in creatione & conservatione rerum ostenderit, cur non etiam libertatis suæ? Quæ affinitas inter voces & rerum conceptus? Et tamen sola consuetudine nexum inter se tàm arctum acquiruntut se mutuò insequantur prompte. Insuper animus & corpus suis substantijs inter se non minùs differunt quàm suis functionibus; Si proinde qui nobis adversantur volunt animum & corpus suis substantiis conjungi posse, quare non & functionibus? Qui accidentia realia admittunt non dubitant quin ista accidetia in corpus agere queant, cùm tamen majus inter utraque, hoc est, inter accidentia & substantiam, quàm inter duas substantias sit discrimen; Proinde absurdum ne esto ex varijs organorum corporeorum motibus varias oriri in animo cogitationes, & viciflim ex varijs cogitationibus varias in corpore excitari motus.
units.tr: You object thirdly: since the soul differs from its body in its whole kind, its functions also differ in their whole kind from the functions of its body. How then can the functions of the soul have a connection with the functions of the body, by which it is said to be united to the body? I answer: I grant that the functions of the soul and of the body differ in their whole kind from one another. Hence nature cannot couple them, but the power of the divine will alone joins them into one union. The philosopher should not be ashamed to flee at times to this will of God as to a sacred anchor. For how does it happen that my ball, after it has pushed yours from its place, does not go on moving as quickly as before, although it has given nothing of its motion to yours, since an accident does not pass from one subject to another? Certainly in solving this question we must have recourse to the will of God, saying that God established the law of nature so that a body which drives another from its place gives up of its own motion just as much as the other has received. If you seek another cause of this law than the will of God, you will labour in vain, because for laws of nature, since they are first principles, there is no other explanation. And since God has displayed traces of his other perfections in the creation and preservation of things, why not also of his freedom? What affinity is there between the words and the concepts of things? And yet by custom alone such a close connection has been acquired between them that they promptly follow one another. Moreover, the soul and the body differ from one another in their substances no less than in their functions. If therefore those who oppose us want the soul and body to be joined in their substances, why not also in their functions? Those who admit real accidents do not doubt that these accidents can act upon the body, although the difference between the two, that is, between accidents and substance, is greater than between two substances. Therefore let it not be absurd that from various motions of the bodily organs various thoughts arise in the soul, and conversely that from various thoughts various motions are excited in the body.
XXXVI.

units.la: Non dubito quin qui hæc attentè meditabuntur circa unionem animi cum corpore intelligendam difficultates adhuc habeant maximas; Sciant verò quòd meditatione se faciant ineptos ad unionem hanc cognoscendam, quia quæ cognoscenda sunt ut unita, eo modo cognoscenda sunt quo cognoscuntur ut unum, ut unitorum differentia confundatur; Ipsa vero unionis animi cum corpore meditatio rerum unitarum tantas protrudit differetias, ut earum diligens inspectio impediat quo minus ut unum cognosci possint; proinde ad unionem animi cum corpore cognoscendam ea cogitandi forma utendum est, quæ caret omni attentione, quomodo videmus avium volatum, sylvarum discrimina, hortorum anfractus; Hinc affirmo quod qui meditationibus nunquam vacarunt ad unionem animi cum corpore cognoscendam sint omnium paratissimi; Meditabundi enim attentione, quâ vix ac ne vix quidem superseedere possunt, omnia secant, & animi cum corpore unionem examinaturi naturas potius distinguunt quam confundant: Observando corpus humanum quod sentiat & quod sua voluntate se huc illuc movere possit rite cognoscitur ipsa animi cum corpore unio, quia animus & corpus cognoscuntur ea ratione ut unum; Nec solo intellectu ad hanc unionem cognoscendam est utendum, quia purus intellectus animum cum corpore non confundit, sed potius ab eo distinguit; Neq; imaginatione utendum est, quia corpus cum animo etiam non confundit sed ab eo maxime distinguit. Hinc factum ut Nobilissimus Cartesius puro intellectui paucos suæ ætatis dies, imaginationi pauciores horas, reliquum veri sui otij solis dederit sensibus, ut ad quodvis suo modo cognoscendum habilis foret. Interim fateor quod conjunctio, quâ corpus corpori est unitum, eo accuratius cognoscatur quo attentius unitorum natura perpenditur, quia eo nexu inter se cohærent, quem naturalis eorum conditio requirit; Conjunctio vero, quæ animo cum corpore suo intercedit, ea conjungit quæ conjungi suâ natura repugnant, ut qui unita attentè consideratʼ non conjunctionem sed conjungi repugnantiam deprehendat.
units.tr: I do not doubt that those who meditate on these things attentively, in trying to understand the union of the soul with the body, will still have the greatest difficulties. But let them know that by meditating they make themselves unfit for knowing this union, because things that are to be known as united must be known in the way they are known as one, so that the difference of the united things is confused. Indeed, the very meditation on the union of the soul with the body brings forward such great differences among united things that a careful inspection of them hinders them from being known as one. Therefore, in order to know the union of the soul with the body, we must use that form of thinking which lacks all attention, as we see the flight of birds, the distinctions of woods, and the windings of gardens. Hence I affirm that those who have never given themselves to meditations are the most ready of all to know the union of the soul with the body. For those who meditate, with an attention which they can scarcely or not at all lay aside, cut up everything, and when about to examine the union of the soul with the body, they distinguish its natures rather than confuse them. By observing that the human body feels, and that it can move itself hither and thither by its will, the union of the soul with the body is rightly known, because the soul and the body are known in this way as one. Nor should we use the intellect alone to know this union, because pure intellect does not confuse the soul with the body but rather distinguishes it from the body. Nor should we use the imagination, because it too does not confuse the body with the soul but distinguishes it from the soul most of all. Hence it came about that the most noble Descartes gave to pure intellect a few days of his life, to imagination fewer hours, and the rest of his true leisure to the senses alone, so that he might be fit to know each thing in its own way. Meanwhile I grant that the conjunction by which one body is united to another is known the more accurately the more attentively the nature of the united things is weighed, because they cohere with one another by the bond which their natural condition requires. But the conjunction which lies between the soul and its own body joins things which by their nature repel being joined, so that one who attentively considers the united things finds not a conjunction but a repugnance to being joined.
XXXVII.

units.la: Objicis Quarto; Unio animi cum corpore est arctissima unio, quæ proindè sola virtutis activæ & passivæ cooperatione non potest absolvi. Respondeo; Cooperatio virtutis activæ & passivæ, quæ inter animum & corpus facit vinculum, quò ligantur, arctissimum. 1. Quia eôpse momento, quò animus agit vel corpus, vel corpus vel animus afficitur; Sic eodem ipsò momento, quo corpus vulneratur, animus inde afficitur; Eôpse etiam momentò, quò pedi motum animus imperat, movetur pes. 2. Quia neq; animus in corpus neq; corpus in animum agit quin vice versa vel in animum vel corpus agatur; Ita animus pedibus motum imperare non potest quin animus eô ipsò momento inde ita afficiaturur motum sentiat. 3. Animus à corpore & vicissim corpus ab animo nõ uno, sed pluribus quàm dici potest, modis afficitur, qui cùm sint totidem contactus, manifestũ est quòd animus corpori & vicissim animo corpus multò arctiùs uniatur quàm corpus corpori adunari possit, quia quantumvis arctè corpus conjungatur corpori tamen extremis tantùm partibus perficitur conjunctio, cùm corporum penetratio fieri non possit. 4. Quia ipso corpore benè vel malè affectò, etiam ipse animus benè vel malè inde habet, quæ compassio non nisi inter amicos arctissimè conjunctos contingere potest; Sic læsò capite læditur & animus non quidem vulnere sed dolore. 5. Quia corporis commoda vel incommoda sentit animus tanquàm sua ipsius; Sic animus pedis læsionem tanquàm suam ipsius læsionem sentit; Inde factum ut communiter sensum parti vulneratæ, hoc est, pedi tribuerint; Unde illa nomina & phrases, Cephalalgia, Odontalgia, Cardialgia, doleo pedibus, &c. 6. Quia sensuum perceptiones, quibus animus animadvertit motus in corpore factos, sunt ita obscurae, ut motus non ut motus percipiatur, verum ut aliud quid, quod quale sit nescimus; Quae confuse percipiendi ratio animum cum corpore confundit, quia animus se solo utens distincte percipit quaecunque percipit.
units.tr: You object fourthly: the union of soul with body is a most close union, and so cannot be explained by the cooperation of active and passive power alone. I reply: the cooperation of active and passive power, which forms the bond between soul and body, binds them most closely. (1) At the very moment the soul acts on the body, or the body is acted upon, the soul is affected in turn; so at the very moment the body is wounded, the soul is affected by it, and at the very moment the soul commands the foot to move, the foot moves. (2) The soul cannot act on the body without the body acting on the soul at the same moment, or the reverse; so the soul cannot command the feet to move without being affected by that movement at the same instant and perceiving it. (3) The soul is affected by the body, and the body by the soul, not in one way but in more ways than can be told; since these are as many points of contact, it is plain that soul and body are united far more closely than one body can be joined to another, because however tightly one body is joined to another, the joining is made only at the extremities, since the penetration of bodies is impossible. (4) When the body is well or ill affected, the soul too is well or ill affected by it; such sympathy can occur only between friends most closely joined. Thus when the head is hurt, the soul is hurt too, not by a wound but by pain. (5) The soul feels the body's advantages or disadvantages as its own; so the soul feels the injury to the foot as its own injury. Hence people commonly ascribe the sensation to the injured part, that is, to the foot; whence those names and phrases: headache, toothache, heartache, "I hurt in my feet," and so on. (6) The perceptions of the senses, by which the soul notices motions made in the body, are so obscure that the motion is perceived not as motion but as something else, of what kind we do not know; this confused way of perceiving confounds the soul with the body, since the soul, using itself alone, perceives distinctly whatever it perceives.
XXXVIII.

units.la: Objicis Quinto; Animus meditationi rerum sublimium admodum intentus, negligit suum corpus nec observat ea quae corpus afficiunt; Ergo durante tam profunda meditatione animus erit a corpore separatus. Respondeo animus a corpore eo casu revera est seperatus; Unde patet cur Plato Philosophiam mortis meditationem appellaverit; Quanto enim profundius ac diutius philosophamur, tanto magis animum a corpore abstrahimus, sentire atque ab externis affici desuescimus, & gratae contemplationi indulgentes, pedum frigus sedentes, cibi saporem comedentes, assidentium gestus & voces oculis atque auribus instructi ac praesentes quandoque non percipimus; Nec inde sequitur Ecstaticos & Epilepticos desinere esse homines; Tum quia Apostolus Paulus quanquam Epistola posteriore ad Corinth. duodecimo dubitet an animus suus revera a corpore fuerit separatus non tamen dubitat sibi homini raptum illu contigisse; Tum quia homo definit esse homo quando corpus ita vitiatur ut suo modo movere & moveri amplius nequeat, ita enim fit ut animus animum ad suum corpus revertendi abjiciat; Quamdiu autem animus revertendi manet, homo non definit esse homo; Quemadmodum dum dùm lampas non putatur extincta quantisper flammula subindè recurrens non nihil olei iambendo pergit absumere; Columbæ & apes ex consuetudine abire, & redire solent, ex jurisconsultorum sententia eousq; nostræ manent donec animum revertendi habent.
units.tr: You object fifthly: the soul, very intent on meditating on lofty things, neglects its body and does not notice what affects the body; therefore, while it is engaged in such deep meditation, the soul will be separated from the body. I reply that in that case the soul is indeed separated from the body. Hence it is plain why Plato called philosophy a meditation on death. For the more deeply and the longer we philosophize, the more we draw the soul away from the body, and the more we grow unaccustomed to sensing and being affected by external things. Indulging in pleasing contemplation, we sometimes do not perceive the cold of our feet as we sit, the taste of the food we eat, or the gestures and voices of those sitting beside us, though they are before our eyes and ears. Nor does it follow from this that ecstatics and epileptics cease to be human. First, because the Apostle Paul, though in his later Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter twelve) he doubts whether his soul was truly separated from the body, does not doubt that this rapture happened to him as a man. Second, because a man ceases to be a man when the body is so damaged that it can no longer move and be moved in its own way; for then the soul gives up the intention of returning to its body. As long as the soul keeps the intention of returning, however, the man does not cease to be a man. It is like a lamp: it is not thought to be extinguished, since a little flame that flickers up now and then keeps on consuming some oil by licking at it. Doves and bees commonly go away and come back, and according to the opinion of the jurists they remain ours as long as they have the intention of returning.
XXXIX.

units.la: Obijcis Sextο; Act. 20. de Eutycho jam mortuo Apostolus Paulus ait, ne turbemini, anima enim ipsius in ipso est, Ergo anima in corpore suo aliam etiam præsentiam habet quàm quæ sit tantùm activæ & passivæ virtutis; Nam in Eutycho activæ & passivæ virtutis operatio cessabat cùm fuerit mortuus, & tamē anima in ipso adhuc dicitur fuisse. Resp. Apostolus his verbis, anima enim ipsius in ipso est, non vult indicare ab ipso corpore Eutychi animam non recessisse, sic enim miraculum Apostolus negaret quò mortuus in vitam fuit revocatus; Verba enim Apostoli continent consolationem quâ auditorum Eutychi inopinâ morte consternatorum animos refocillare studet; Consolationem autem, sensu objectionis stante, continere non possunt quin aperte negent miraculum. Explicari autem commodè possunt dicendo quòd Apostolus ea pronuntiaverit aut in ipso editi miraculi momento, aut quòd de re mox secuturâ certissimus esset.
units.tr: You object sixthly: in Acts 20, of Eutychus, already dead, the Apostle Paul says, "Do not be troubled, for his soul is in him". Therefore the soul in the body has some other presence than merely that of active and passive power; for in Eutychus the operation of active and passive power had ceased when he died, and yet the soul is said still to be in him. Reply: the Apostle, in these words, "for his soul is in him", does not mean to indicate that the soul of Eutychus had not departed from his body; for in that case the Apostle would be denying the miracle by which he was raised from the dead. The Apostle's words contain a consolation, by which he seeks to revive the spirits of the hearers, who were dismayed by Eutychus's unexpected death. But if the sense of the objection stands, these words cannot contain a consolation without plainly denying the miracle. They can, however, be conveniently explained by saying that the Apostle spoke either at the very moment of the miracle that was performed, or because he was quite certain of the thing that was about to follow soon.
XL.

units.la: Quæris ubi Eutychi animus fuerit postquàm è corpore excesserat? Resp. erat ubi cogitabat; ut si res de quibus cogitabat nuspiàm fuerunt, nec animus Eutychi uspiàm fuerit, quomodò animus nuspiàm est quando sola suiipsius contemplatione vivit; Si verò res, quibus cogitandis animus occupabatur, alicubi fuerunt, ibidem animus Eutychi erat, quia animus pro naturæ suæ conditione rebus aliter vicinus, quàm de ijs cogitando, esse non poteft; Et quæ animo, quatenus est cogitans, sunt præsentia ea ipsi revera sunt præsentia, quippe animus nihil aliud est quàm substantia cogitans; Quomodo enim quicquam animo potest esse vicinum nisi de eo cogitet? Appone homini quicquid velis, nisi de eo cogitet, animo prope admotum dici non potest; Contra remove ab homine quicquid velis quamdiu de eo animus cogitare non cessat ei adhuc est revera præsens. Deinde animus trahit res in suam viciniam, quas extra se habet, per solas ideas, quas de ijs format; atqui animus rerum ideas habens est de rebus cogitans; Ergo res animo non fiunt propinquæ nisi quatenus ei cogitanti obversantur. Præterea si animus per somnium videt sibi coronam regiam contigisse cum applausu totius populi lætatur impendiò; An animus, si in multos annos tale somnium duraret, tantò tempore non æquè foret felix ac ille cujus capiti revera corona imponitur? Proinde concludendum animo per somnium non minùs, verè propinquas fieri res ac quandò vigilat; Atqui somnium quid est nisi cogitatio?
units.tr: You ask where the soul of Eutychus was after it had departed from the body? I answer: it was where it was thinking. For if the things about which it was thinking were nowhere, then the soul of Eutychus was nowhere either, since a soul is nowhere when it lives only by contemplating itself. But if the things with which the soul was occupied in thinking were somewhere, then the soul of Eutychus was in that same place, because by the nature of the soul it cannot be near things in any way other than by thinking about them. Things are present to the soul, as it is a thinking thing, really present to it, since the soul is nothing other than a thinking substance. For how can anything be near the soul unless it thinks about it? Set before a man whatever you like: unless he thinks about it, it cannot be said to be brought near to his soul. On the contrary, remove from a man whatever you like: as long as the soul does not cease to think about it, it is still really present to him. Further, the soul draws into its neighbourhood the things it has outside itself, through the ideas alone which it forms of them; but the soul that has ideas of things is thinking about things. Therefore things do not become near to the soul except insofar as they are before it in thought. Moreover, if in a dream the soul sees that a royal crown has been placed on its head, and it rejoices greatly at the applause of the whole people, would not the soul, if such a dream lasted for many years, be just as happy over so long a time as he on whose head the crown is really placed? Therefore it must be concluded that in a dream things are made really near to the soul no less than when it is awake. But what is a dream, if not thought?
XLI.

units.la: Causa cur putant animo res viciniores fieri posse quàm per solas cogitationes, est quia hoc præjudicio laborant ferè omnes, animo nihil posse esse præsens, nisi corpori sit prius præsens, ita putant coronam regiam non esse verè præsentem nisi capiti reapse imponatur, à manu aut pede tangatur, aut ipsos moveat oculos, perperàm præsentiam corporis cum præsentia animi confundentes; Quidquid corpori præsens est, idmenti plerumq; est præsens, sed quomodò corpori? quia ab eo tägitur; Quomodò menti? Quia de eo cogitat, e.g. hæc ipsa mensa cui nunc assideo, præsens est corpori, quia illam cubito utroq; tango; Animo etiam est præsens, quatenus mihi videor videre vel tangere mensam, id quod est de mensa cogitare.
units.tr: The reason why they think things can become nearer to the soul than through thoughts alone is that almost everyone labours under this prejudice: that nothing can be present to the soul unless it is first present to the body. Thus they think the royal crown is not really present unless it is actually placed on the head, touched by a hand or foot, or unless it moves the eyes themselves; they wrongly confuse the presence of the body with the presence of the soul. Whatever is present to the body is generally present to the mind as well; but how is it present to the body? Because it acts upon it. How is it present to the mind? Because the mind thinks of it. For example, this very table at which I now sit is present to my body, because I touch it with both elbows. It is also present to my soul, insofar as I seem to myself to see or touch the table, which is to think about the table.
XLII.

units.la: Objicis Septimo; Epist: posteriore ad Corinth.12. Apostolus Paulus facta narratione revelationis rerum Cœlestium sibi factæ ait se nescire an in corpore an extra corpus sibi tàm gloriosa contigerit manifestatio; Ergo Apostolus dubitans an in corpore ea sibi facta fuerit revelatio præsupponit animum rebus sublimibus intentissimum esse posse absq; recessu ex corpore; Idque locum habet sive per phrasin, an in corpore, Apostolus dubitet an in corpore in cœlum translato sive an in corpore terris affixo sibi arcanorum divinorum revelatio contigerit. Respondeo, primò Verba Apostoli in hoc loco veritati præjudicare non possunt, sunt enim prosecta ex principijs, quibus Apostolus vel à præceptoribus vel ab aliis fuit imbutus, sunt verba cum ignorantiæ non scientiæ professione. secundò; Verba Apostoli apprimè nobis inserviunt, utrovis sensu phrasis an in corpore sumatur; Quia Apostolus dubitans an animus ecstaticus an reapse in cœlum translatus tantâ fuerit fruitus gloriâ, evidenter concludendum præbet gloriam cœlestem animo per cogitationes revera posse manifestari, quia gloriâ cœli animus ecstaticus frui non potest nisi per cogitationes; Animus verò in cœlum translatus gloriâ fruitur reapse; Ergò Apostolus dubitare non potuisset an animus ecstaticus an in cœlum translatus tantâ fuisset fruitus gloriâ nisi præsupponeret ecstatico manifestari gloriam cœli posse eâ ratione ut animus nesciat an sibi per ecstasin an verò per translationem in cœlum tanta obtigerit gloria; Id quod est gloriam cœli verè manifestari.
units.tr: You object, seventh, from the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 12: the Apostle Paul, after giving an account of the revelation of heavenly things made to him, says that he does not know whether that such great manifestation came to him in the body or outside the body. Therefore the Apostle, doubting whether that revelation was made to him in the body, presupposes that the mind can be most intent upon sublime things without withdrawing from the body. And this holds whether the phrase "in the body" is taken to mean that the Apostle doubts whether the revelation came to him in the body carried up into heaven, or whether it came to him while his body was still fixed to the earth. I answer: first, the words of the Apostle in this place cannot prejudice the truth, for they proceed from principles with which the Apostle was imbued either by his teachers or by others; they are words of a profession of ignorance, not of knowledge. Second, the words of the Apostle serve us very well, whichever sense the phrase "in the body" is taken in. For since the Apostle doubts whether the ecstatic mind, or the mind really carried up into heaven, enjoyed so great a glory, it is clearly to be concluded that the heavenly glory can truly be made manifest to the mind through thoughts, because an ecstatic mind cannot enjoy the glory of heaven except through thoughts. But a mind carried up into heaven really enjoys the glory. Therefore the Apostle could not have doubted whether the ecstatic mind or the mind carried up into heaven had enjoyed so great a glory, unless he presupposed that the glory of heaven could be made manifest to the ecstatic mind in such a way that the mind did not know whether such great glory had come to it through ecstasy or through translation into heaven. This is to say that the glory of heaven is truly made manifest.
XLIII.

units.la: Objicis Octavo; Lucæ 16. legimus quòd Lazari animus ab Angelis fuit in sinum Abrahæ asportatus; Ergò animus mutare potest loca ut modò hîc modò sit ibi non tantùm operative sed etiam quoad situm; Id enim quod transfit de loco in locum motu locali situm admittit: proinde absurdum non est animi u in suo corpore habere suum situm. Resp. I. Absurdum est animo tribuere motum.
units.tr: You object, eighthly: we read in Luke 16 that the soul of Lazarus was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. Therefore the soul can change places, so that it is now here and now there, not only operatively but also in respect of position. For that which passes from place to place admits position through local motion. Hence it is not absurd that the soul has its position in its body. Answer: I. It is absurd to attribute motion to the soul.

units.la: 1. Quia si animus è corpore suo recedit exibit vel per aures vel per oculos vel per os. Atqui nulla est causa cur per unam corporis partem potiùs exeat quàm per aliam. Ergò per nullam exit. 2. Scire vellem quò motu ex corpore exeat versus cœlum an motu spirali? Si motu spirali imitabitur volatum avium quæ hoc motu sursùm tolluntur facilius quàm quòvis aliò; Si motu rectò, id fiet ut compendiò utatur, ad lineam autem rectam, quæ tantæ longitudinis, ducendam dexteritate mathematica majore opus est quàm in hac vita obtineri possit. 3. Quantumvis velox fuerit motus, quò animus migrare dicitur in cœlum, patietur tamen aliquid moræ in emetienda via, tùm quia omnis motus est successivus, tùm quia viæ longitudo est maxima; Sic animus tantò itinere utens neq; est in terra neq; in cœlis sed in loco intermedio; Id quod purgatorio non parùm patrocinatur; Si animo velis gloriæ lumen affundi eôpse momentò quò corpus egreditur ut cœlitibus jam annumerari possit, nostræ causæ litas, sic enim animus migrationibus quærere gloriam opus non habet. 4. Quid illa migratio juvat cùm animus fieri gloriosus non possit nisi gloriosis cogitationibus? Ejusmodi autem cogitationum plenè particeps esse potest, quanquàm migrationes de loco in locum non instituat, 5. Stulta opinio quòd animus in cœlum transfeat feat instar viatoris causam dedit consuetudini mulierculilarum qua fenestras aperiunt, ut animus e corpore humano recedens liberius obstacula pervadere possit; Et quanquam doctiores respondeant animum penetrare corpora ut necesse non sit aperire fenestram tamen intellectu non assequuntur quae dicunt, sc. quomodo substantia motu suo penetrare substantiam possit. 6. Scire etiam velim an animus seipsum moveat an moveatur ab alio? Si prius cur non subinde ex corpore exspatiatur imprimis quando corpus aegrotat? Si posterius, quid illud fit a quo animus impelli possit nemo hominum intelligit. 7. Insuper motus concessus est rebus ut remotis possint fieri vicinae; Atqui animus absq; motu locali rebus fit vicinus; Ergo nullus usus motus. II. Ex loco allegato Lucae definire non est animi naturam; Tum quia ibi parabolica continetur recitatio, quae non nisi ex fine est argumentativa, finis autem parabolae non est animi a corpore separati enodare naturam; Sed indicare quod bonis post hanc vitam bene, malis male fit futurum, & quod horum & illorum status inter se permutari nunquam patientur; Tum quia animabus separatis oculos, digitos, linguam, sitim & colloquia locus tribuit, quae animabus separatis convenire non possunt. III. Asportatio animi Lazari in sinum Abrahae facta ab Angelis est metaphorica, quemadmodum sinus Abrahae sensum metaphoricum habet, ut sensus fit quod anima Lazari in laetitiae coelestis usum cum Abrahamo communem devenerit; Haec transportatio dicitur facta ab Angelis itidem figurate, quia nec animus portari, nec Angeli portare possunt, cum onera portentur humeris, capiti vel pectori imposita; Sed Angeli asportarunt animum Lazari in finum Abrahæ quandò animam Lazari folenni jubilo in gloriæ communionem adoptárunt, Luc: 15. verf. 10.
units.tr: 1. For if the soul withdraws from its body, it will go out either through the ears, the eyes or the mouth. But there is no cause why it should leave by one part of the body rather than another. Therefore it leaves by none. 2. I should like to know by what motion it leaves the body towards heaven: a spiral motion? If by a spiral motion, it will imitate the flight of birds, which are lifted upward by this motion more easily than by any other. If by a straight motion, it will do so in order to take a shortcut, but drawing a straight line of such length requires greater mathematical skill than can be attained in this life. 3. However swift the motion by which the soul is said to migrate to heaven, it will nevertheless suffer some delay in traversing the way, both because every motion is successive and because the length of the way is very great. Thus the soul, making such a journey, is neither on earth nor in heaven but in an intermediate place, which lends no small support to purgatory. If you wish the light of glory to be poured upon the soul at the very moment the body leaves it, so that it may already be numbered among the heavenly inhabitants, you concede our case, for in that way the soul has no need to seek glory by migrations. 4. What good does that migration do, since the soul cannot become glorious except through glorious thoughts? Yet it can fully share in such thoughts without undertaking migrations from place to place. 5. The foolish opinion that the soul passes into heaven like a traveller has given rise to the custom of old women who open windows, so that the soul departing from the human body may pass through obstacles more freely. Although more learned men reply that the soul penetrates bodies, so that there is no need to open a window, they do not grasp with their understanding what they are saying, namely how one substance can penetrate another by its own motion. 6. I should also like to know whether the soul moves itself or is moved by another. If the former, why does it not then wander out of the body from time to time, especially when the body is sick? If the latter, no man understands what that is by which the soul can be impelled. 7. Moreover, motion is granted to things so that those that are remote may become near. But the soul becomes near to things without local motion. Therefore motion is of no use to it. II. The passage of Luke cited does not define the nature of the soul; first, because it contains a parabolic narrative, which is argumentative only as to its purpose, and the purpose of a parable is not to unfold the nature of the soul separated from the body, but to indicate that it will go well after this life for the good and ill for the wicked, and that the states of these and those will never be exchanged; second, because the place assigns to separated souls eyes, fingers, a tongue, thirst and conversations, which cannot belong to separated souls. III. The carrying of the soul of Lazarus into Abraham's bosom by the angels is metaphorical, just as Abraham's bosom has a metaphorical sense, in that the soul of Lazarus came to share in heavenly joy in common with Abraham. This transport is likewise said to be made by the angels figuratively, because neither can a soul be carried nor can angels carry it, since burdens are borne on the shoulders, head or chest. But the angels carried the soul of Lazarus into Abraham's bosom when they received the soul of Lazarus into the fellowship of glory with solemn rejoicing, Luc. 15. v. 10.
XLIV.

units.la: Quanquàm animo res, de quibus cogitat, revera sint præsentes, aliæ tamen magis quàm aliæ; Quò enim pluribus cogitationibus circa res animus versatur eò sunt ei præsentiores; Sic res, quam animus non tantùm cognoscit sed etiam amat, præsentior est animo quàm quæ ab ipso duntaxat cognoscitur; Arctior autem animi cum rebus conjunctio non datur quàm quâ animus corpus sibi unit; Quia res, de quibus animus cogitat, quâ ratione cunq; mutentur; mutationem tamen animo nullam inferunt, nec vice versâ; Animi autem cum corpore colligatio hoc habet ut corpore variationem patiente patiatur & animus & vice versâ; Ubi in agendo & patiendo mutuus concursus haud dubiè animum cum corpore multò arctiùs copulat quàm cogitans cum re cogitata copuletur.
units.tr: Although the things of which the soul thinks are really present to it, some are more present than others. For the more numerous the thoughts with which the soul is occupied about a thing, the more present that thing is to it. Thus a thing which the soul not only knows but also loves is more present to the soul than one which it merely knows. But no closer union of the soul with things is given than that by which the soul is united to its body. For the things about which the soul thinks, however they may be changed, bring no change to the soul, nor the reverse; whereas the bond between soul and body has this feature: when the body undergoes a change, the soul suffers too, and vice versa. Where there is such mutual concourse in acting and suffering, this undoubtedly joins the soul to the body far more closely than the thinker is joined to the thing thought.
XLV.

units.la: Ex superioribus ergò liquet animum toti corpori & singulis ejus partibus esse conjunctum, tùm quia animus & toti corpori & singulis ejus partibus seorsim motum imperare potest, tùm quia & à toto corpore & à singulis ejus partibus seorsim affici animus solet; Quemadmodùm enim animus toti corpori imperat ut ad sessionem sese componat, aut oculis seorsim ut Soli sese obvertant; Sic animus non à sola totius corporis sessione, sed etiam seorsim ab oculorum motu affici potest.
units.tr: It is therefore clear from what has been said above that the soul is joined to the whole body and to each of its parts, both because the soul can command motion in the whole body and in its individual parts separately, and because the soul is accustomed to be affected both by the whole body and by its individual parts separately. For just as the soul commands the whole body to compose itself for sitting, or commands the eyes separately to turn themselves towards the sun, so the soul can be affected not only by the sitting of the whole body but also separately by the movement of the eyes.
XLVI.

units.la: Interim animus præcipuè conjunctus est glandulæ pineali; Quia quanquàm nobis sint duo oculi, duæ aures, duæ manus, atq; ita duplciia sint externorum sensuum organa, quemadmodum & partes cerebri omnes geminæ, sensus tamen unius cujusque rei unô tempore tantùm est unus; Necesse enim est existere locum aliquem, in quo duæ impressiones per duplicia sensuum organa ab unico venientes objecto rursus in unum coëant antequàm perveniant ad animam, ne ipsi loco unius obje-cti duo objecta repræsentent; Nullus verò in toto corpore humano locus invenitur ubi ejusmodi coitio fieri possit nisi in cerebri meditullio ubi glandula est pinealis; Sicuti enim è colo fila hûç illûc trahuntur â netrice, ita è cerebro nervi, sensuum proxima organa, in omnes partes corporis nostri protenduntur. Nec putandum est quòd in glandula pineali situm animus habeat, sed in ea proximè atq; immediatè suas functiones exercet agendo & patiendo, motus scil. corporis alios imperando alias sentiendo; Unô verbô, animo proxima sedes est in glandula pineali non situs sed functionum ratione; Proindè quandò pes dicitur dolere, dolor non in pede sed cerebri est meditullio, dolor enim pedis est sensatio quâ animus in cerebri meditullio per nervorû ad pedem protensorum beneficium obscurè sentit lesionem pedis tanquàm suam & in pede existentem.
units.tr: Yet the soul is especially joined to the pineal gland. For although we have two eyes, two ears, two hands, and thus the organs of the external senses are double, as are all the parts of the brain, yet the sense of any one thing is only one at a single time. For there must necessarily exist some place in which the two impressions, received through the double sense organs from a single object, come together again into one before they reach the soul, lest they present two objects in place of one. But no place in the whole human body is found where such a coming together can take place except the middle of the brain, where the pineal gland is. For just as threads are drawn hither and thither from the distaff by the spinner, so from the brain the nerves, the organs nearest to the senses, are stretched out into all parts of our body. Nor should it be thought that the soul has its seat in the pineal gland, but it exercises its functions most closely and immediately there, by acting and being acted upon, namely by commanding the bodily movements and by perceiving others. In a word, the soul's nearest seat is in the pineal gland not as a place but in respect of its functions. Hence, when the foot is said to hurt, the pain is not in the foot but in the middle of the brain; for the pain of the foot is a sensation by which the soul, in the middle of the brain, dimly perceives through the agency of the nerves stretched to the foot the injury to the foot as its own and as existing in the foot.
XLVII.

units.la: Ut extra oleas vagentur qui quærunt an anima sit in tota glandula an in parte ejus? Quia animus, cùm non situs sed functionum ratione in glandula esse dicatur, neq; cum totius glandulæ neq; cum partis occupatione in glandula est; Mirum est quòd adversarij quodvis in cerebro punctum potiùs animo esse sedem voluntquàm glandulam pinealem, omni ratione destituti; Absur-ditasurditatem suæ produnt opinionis, tum quòd animo se designare sedem opinantes nullam designant, tum quòd puncta à corporum communione, quanquàm ex illis omnia constent corpora, excludere coguntur metuentes ne puncta corporibus accensendo dimensionem animi sedes habeat; Discant nullas inter corpus & spiritum medias dari substantias.
units.tr: So let those who ask whether the soul is in the whole of the pineal gland or only in a part of it go wander beyond the olive groves. For the soul is said to be in the gland not by place but by the manner of its functions, so it is present in the gland neither by occupying the whole of it nor by occupying a part of it. It is strange that the opponents, bereft of every reason, prefer that some point in the brain rather than the pineal gland be the soul's seat. They betray the absurdity of their opinion: first, because in thinking they assign a seat to the soul, they in fact assign none; second, because they are forced to exclude points from the communion of bodies, although all bodies consist of such points, fearing that if points were counted among bodies, the soul's seat would have dimension. Let them learn that there are no intermediate substances between body and spirit.
§ ornamental rule

units.la: I. Ornatissimo atq; Doctissimo Dn. Defendenti.
units.tr: I. To the most distinguished and most learned Mr. Defender.

units.la: Dulcia non meruit, qui non gustavit amara: Sic Tibi sudanti jam dulcia præmia confert Musa; Dies noctesq; sonant, en! digna merenti! Junxisti studiis animum, quem æquabit Olympo Laude Minerva.
units.tr: He has not earned sweet things who has not tasted bitter ones. So the Muse now brings sweet rewards to you as you sweat; day and night resound, behold, worthy rewards for one who deserves them! You have joined to your studies a mind that Minerva will match to Olympus in praise.

units.la: Indissolubilis amicitiæ tesseram, scripsit Musâ & Apolline nullo, Joh. Casp. Seelmatter.
units.tr: A token of indissoluble friendship, written with no Muse and no Apollo, by Joh. Casp. Seelmatter.

units.la: II. Acclamatio Annagrammatico echica CORNELIUS HENTZIUS. Ἀναγραμματισμὸς. VIRTUS ZELO HISCENS.
units.tr: II. Acclamation in echo verse, in anagram form, by CORNELIUS HENTZIUS. Anagrammatism [Ἀναγραμματισμὸς]. VIRTUS ZELO HISCENS (Virtue yawning with zeal).

units.la: ECho responde dulces quem quæro Camenæ? Mene rogas? Respondebis qua Mente? Libente; Nonne sacri Suadæ Tripodes hunc Edocuere? Vere; Virtutis raræ num Zelj glíscit Amore? More; sed hinc quæso dic quanta feret Bona? Dona. Multane dona Feret? Meret; en in nomine Zelum? Coelum? Nam novit cœli perrumpere Fores. O Res! Vox resonans nunc plura Tacebo; Valebo.
units.tr: Echo answers: whom do I seek, sweet Muse? Me, do you ask? Will you answer with what mind? Willingly. Have not the holy tripods of Persuasion taught him this? Truly. Does he burn with love of rare virtue? Manifestly. But tell me, I ask, what great goods will it bring? Gifts. Will it bring many gifts? It deserves them. Then is zeal in the name? Heaven? For he knows how to break through the gates of heaven. O thing! Resounding voice, now I shall say little; I shall farewell.
Appended to the emblem of a brotherhood that will last forever.
Joh. Rodolphus Salchlinus.
